items.body:
Rachael Yamagata has never been just a heartbreak singer. Across two decades, the Hudson Valley-based singer-songwriter has built a world around bruising vulnerability, cinematic songwriting, wry humour, and a voice that feels like it knows exactly what you are trying not to say out loud.

That is why her return to Singapore feels special. Happening on 16 September at Foo Chow Hall, the concert marks her first gig here since 2018, her 10th Singapore performance, and her only Southeast Asia stop for this tour.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Mailive (@mailive_damai)

For longtime fans, it is a long-awaited reunion. For casual listeners who found her through TV show OSTs, or a late-night playlist that knew too much, it is the perfect time to dive deeper.

From early Happenstance favourites to K-drama-defining soundtrack moments and her latest chapter on Starlit Alchemy, here are 10 Rachael Yamagata songs every fan should know.

1. ‘Be Be Your Love’

The gateway song for many Yamagata fans, ‘Be Be Your Love’ remains one of the clearest introductions to her early magic: intimate, aching, direct, and impossible to shake. Taken from her debut album Happenstance, the track captures the emotional push-and-pull that would become central to her songwriting — wanting closeness, fearing the cost, and singing through it anyway.

2. ‘Worn Me Down’

Where ‘Be Be Your Love’ aches, ‘Worn Me Down’ burns. One of the defining cuts from Happenstance, the song brings out Yamagata’s grit — the side of her music that does not just sit in sadness, but pushes back against it. Raw, wounded, and quietly furious, it remains one of her most enduring fan favourites.

3. ‘1963’

‘1963’ shows another side of Yamagata’s early songwriting: playful, sharp, and a little mischievous, while still carrying the emotional charge that runs through Happenstance. It is a reminder that even when her music is filed under heartbreak, there has always been humour, character, and movement in the way she writes.

4. ‘Reason Why’

For fans who love Yamagata at her most stripped-back and vulnerable, ‘Reason Why’ is essential. It feels like a private thought caught at the exact moment it becomes too heavy to keep inside. Less explosive than some of her bigger anthems, but no less devastating, it is a quiet cornerstone of her early catalogue.

5. ‘Elephants’

With Elephants…Teeth Sinking Into Heart, Yamagata deepened the cinematic side of her writing. ‘Elephants’ is slow-moving, heavy, and haunted — the kind of song that makes a whole room go still. It is one of the clearest examples of why her music works so naturally in visual storytelling: every line feels like it belongs to a scene you can already picture.

6. ‘Duet’

Featuring Ray LaMontagne, ‘Duet’ is one of Yamagata’s most beloved collaborations. Tender without being fragile, romantic without feeling neat or simple, the song sits beautifully in that in-between space she does so well — where love is present, but distance is too. It also reflects how far her music has travelled on screen, with her songs appearing across major television series.

7. ‘Something In the Rain’

For many K-drama fans across Asia, this was the song that opened the door. Featured in the hit romance drama Something in the Rain, starring Son Ye-jin and Jung Hae-in, ‘Something In the Rain’ became inseparable from the series’ tender, rain-soaked emotional world. For a new generation of listeners, it was their first encounter with Yamagata’s voice — soft, aching, and instantly memorable.

8. ‘La La La’

Also from Something in the Rain, ‘La La La’ became another defining track from the series. Where ‘Something In the Rain’ carries the ache of longing, ‘La La La’ feels lighter but no less affecting — the kind of song that sounds simple, until it suddenly catches you off guard.

9. ‘No Direction’

Yamagata’s K-drama connection did not stop with Something in the Rain. ‘No Direction’, featured on the soundtrack of One Spring Night, brought her voice into another quietly devastating romance world, this time starring Han Ji-min and Jung Hae-in. It is gentle, searching, and beautifully uncertain — a perfect fit for a story about love arriving when life is already complicated.

10. ‘Carnival’

From Starlit Alchemy, ‘Carnival’ captures Yamagata in a new phase: raw, cinematic, and ready to walk away from everything that no longer fits. Described as an emotional breakthrough, the song feels less like collapse and more like release — a bold, liberating call-to-arms from an artist who has turned grief, surrender, and transformation into her most intentional work yet.

Go deeper

Already know the essentials? Add these to the queue: ‘We Could Still Be Happy’ from One Spring Night, ‘Meet Me By the Water’ from Happenstance, ‘You Won’t Let Me’ from Chesapeake, and Starlit Alchemy cuts ‘Backwards’ and ‘Birds’.

Why Rachael Yamagata still matters today

Yamagata’s music has always found people at turning points — in heartbreak, in grief, in quiet rebuilding, and in the strange middle space between falling apart and finding language for it.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

That is why her songs continue to travel: from albums passed between friends, to scenes in beloved TV series, to K-drama soundtracks that introduced her to a new wave of Asian fans. With Starlit Alchemy, she returns not as an artist revisiting old wounds, but as one transforming them into something bigger, stranger, and more freeing.

Rachael Yamagata: Starlit Alchemy Tour — Live In Singapore is presented by Bandwagon Live, in partnership with The Rock Promotions, MAILIVE, and MAISEAT. Purchase tickets here.

items.body:
Singapore MOAs, your next ride is almost here. Golden Village (GV) has announced that it will exclusively screen TOMORROW X TOGETHER's ENDLESS RIDE VR concert in Singapore, giving fans the chance to experience the group's latest immersive performance from 14 August to 3 September at GV Bugis+.

Produced by AMAZE in collaboration with BIGHIT MUSIC, ENDLESS RIDE marks TOMORROW X TOGETHER's third dedicated VR concert, making the quintet the first K-pop act to release three VR concert productions. Rather than a traditional concert film, the experience places each audience member in an individual VR headset, offering an intimate, first-person perspective of the performances through cinematic storytelling and interactive moments.

Set aboard a dreamlike train journey, the VR concert features performances of fan-favourite tracks including 'LO$ER=LO♡ER', '0X1=LOVESONG (I Know I Love You)', and 'Stick With You'. The production blends immersive visuals with interactive elements designed specifically for virtual reality, creating a viewing experience that goes beyond a standard cinema screening.

The screening is part of Golden Village's growing lineup of alternative entertainment offerings, which has expanded to include concert films, live concert broadcasts, anime, stage productions, and VR experiences as demand for premium event cinema continues to grow.

Fans attending the screenings can also look forward to exclusive collectibles available while stocks last. During the first two weeks, ticket holders will receive random ENDLESS RIDE photo cards, random group photo cards, and an exclusive A5 postcard. Those attending in the final week will receive a random photo frame, a photo card sleeve, and an official ENDLESS RIDE ticket.

Tickets go on sale from 24 July at 3 PM via Golden Village's website, mobile app, and box offices. Prices range from S$38 (GV Movie Club members) to S$40 (Public).

items.body:
Everything's bigger in Texas—including its newest K-pop festival.

KPOPWORLD Festival & Worldwide Dance Competition is making its Texas debut at San Antonio's Alamodome from 28–31 October, bringing together an expansive lineup of artists, one of the world's largest K-pop dance competitions, and a Korean-inspired marketplace for fans across the globe.

Leading the festival's concert lineup are Jay Park, The Rose, SB19, Jessi, ARTMS, CRAVITY, Xdinary Heroes, WONHO, DEAN & Tabber, HEYOON, and DAYOUNG, with more artists set to be announced. Concerts will take place on 30 and 31 October, with doors opening at 3 PM and performances beginning at 6 PM.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Alamodome (@alamodomesa)

Beyond the performances, the four-day event will host the KPOPWORLD Dance Championship, where 32 dance teams representing 29 countries will compete for cash prizes, trophies, and the opportunity to perform on the festival's main stage.

Fans can also explore an International Vendor Village featuring Korean products, exclusive merchandise, collectibles, interactive fan experiences, and themed photo opportunities throughout the festival.

Two-day ticket packages will go on sale on 23 July at 10 AM via the Alamodome website, with prices ranging from US$100 for limited general admission to US$1,200 for Super VIP packages. Single-day tickets will become available after 4 August.

Organisers expect the inaugural festival to draw thousands of fans from across the United States and beyond, giving San Antonio a major tourism boost over Halloween weekend while marking one of the city's biggest K-pop events to date.

items.body:
NewJeans have returned with a surprise film series celebrating their fourth debut anniversary on 22 July, but Danielle’s absence from the release has reignited discussion among fans.

Released after months of limited group activity, the newly filmed content features Minji, Hanni, Haerin, and Hyein in a collection of group and individual videos. It marks the first official content featuring the four members together in two years, following Supernatural.

Set beneath a moonlit summer sky, the group film sees the members gradually enter the frame before holding hands and looking towards the same distant point. Four solo stories also feature references to Bunnies, with bunny-shaped objects and fleeting white silhouettes appearing throughout the dreamlike visuals.

While the release drew millions of views and likes within hours, some fans expressed disappointment over Danielle being left out. Supporters shared the slogan “NewJeans is five”, with one fan writing: “You can’t have a rainbow without the sun.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by NewJeans (@newjeans_official)

ADOR previously announced that it had terminated Danielle’s contract, accusing her of undertaking independent entertainment activities. Danielle and the agency remain involved in a legal dispute.

As the anniversary content arrived, Danielle shared a separate update featuring new photos and a message to fans: “Life gets cloudy sometimes, but the light always finds its way back in. Until then, keep shining.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by @dazzibelle

ADOR described the films as commemorative content created for fans, adding that NewJeans’ future activity plans will be announced once discussions with the members are complete.

items.body:
Over the past few days, the outcry against paper leaks in national examinations (which has resulted in the deaths of 12 - 20 NEET aspirants in 2026, among others) in India and the lack of accountability in government ministers since then has grown into massive protests around the country, with its focal point being at the capital's Jantar Mantar. The massive gathering of youth around the area on June 20 was also met with police brutality, with further reports on subsequent days.

As the protests continue, Jay Drive, the Delhi-based DJ and programmer for adjacent venues Auro Kitchen & Bar and Summerhouse Cafe, has put out an open call to invite DJs, promoters, collectives, artists and other creative industry professionals who can contribute time, equipment or space to come to together for a community fundraiser to take place on Friday, July 24, at Auro Kitchen & Bar.

The fundraiser aims to aid charities and organisations supporting people affected by the brutality meted out at the protests. While further details of the lineup and beneficiaries are locked, people interested in the open call can register their interest of participation by directly messaging Jay Drive on his Instagram.

Image by GigClick

items.excerpt: Across a discography that ranges from politically charged works such as Palestine Is Always War and In the Life of a Palestinian Prisoner to the nostalgic reimagining of Arabic popular song found on Orientalism, Bouncyduck has consistently refused to be defined by a single mood or aesthetic. items.body: Across a discography that ranges from politically charged works such as Palestine Is Always War and In the Life of a Palestinian Prisoner to the nostalgic reimagining of Arabic popular song found on Orientalism, Bouncyduck has consistently refused to be defined by a single mood or aesthetic. His music moves freely between social commentary, cultural memory, humour and personal reflection. It’s Either Me or My Auntie perhaps brings these different strands together most successfully, transforming a beloved Egyptian comedy into a surprisingly moving and deeply life-affirming electronic album. Built from fragments of the film starring Mohamed Henedi, the record turns familiar dialogue into hypnotic techno constructions where humour, memory and repetition become inseparable. Film samples recur like half-remembered conversations, simultaneously comic and unsettling, while Bouncyduck’s finely crafted electronic productions move between house-inflected warmth and increasingly immersive techno rhythms. The result is an album that feels deeply personal without becoming confessional, finding meaning in cultural memory rather than grand statements. Yet beneath its playful surface lie darker undercurrents. Tracks such as “Trauma” carry a palpable sense of anxiety and emotional strain, reflecting the pressures and routines that shaped the album’s creation. The closing “Homeless” is particularly affecting: inspired by the sight of a homeless man searching through rubbish during a winter rainstorm, it channels empathy rather than despair, transforming a moment of social reality into one of the record’s most powerful pieces. Its melodic, Arabic-inflected techno suggests not hopelessness but a heightened awareness of the fragility and value of ordinary life. Given the geopolitical context one might expect a ponderous album. Instead It’s Either Me or My Auntie refuses to separate humour from seriousness. For Bouncyduck, comedy is not an escape from reality but a means of navigating it. The absurdity of the film mirrors the absurdity of lived experience, while repetition becomes a mechanism for endurance rather than entrapment. Even at its most melancholic, the album remains animated by affection and gratitude. In the end, this is a record about survival through culture, memory and laughter. Beneath the loops, and dance rhythms lies an artist finding ways to remain open to the world. For all its darker shadows, It’s Either Me or My Auntie ultimately feels warm and generous. To find out more we reached out to Bouncyduck for an interview conducted over vocal messages on Instagram. But before we get to hear from him directly here’s a mix Bouncyduck has created for Svitlo Radio. Bouncyduck – The Life Of A Survivor Hi Osama, thank you for joining us. Your new album It’s Either Me or My Auntie takes a well-known Egyptian comedy and transforms it into something hypnotic, obsessive, and at times unsettling. What first attracted you to this film, and what made you feel it could serve as the foundation for a techno-oriented experimental record? It’s Either Me or My Auntie has been a part of my life since childhood. I’ve probably watched it sixty times. Every time my grandmother came to visit, I would put on the DVD and watch the film again. It became one of those things that simply stayed with me and became part of who I am. One day, while I was on a bus heading to work, I thought: why not combine techno—the genre I’ve always wanted to make—with the experimental ideas I was interested in, and blend them with my favourite movie? I used to listen to some Japanese experimental records that incorporated advertisements and fragments of found media into the music. I don’t even know what genre you’d call it, but I loved the approach. So I thought, why not do something similar with this film? As for whether I felt the film could serve as the foundation for a techno-oriented experimental record—I honestly never thought about it in those terms. I just did it because it felt right. photo by Bouncyduck Across the album, snippets of dialogue function almost like recurring thoughts rather than narrative elements. The liner notes describe them as “intrusive thoughts” embedded within repetitive structures. How did you approach sampling and manipulating the film’s audio, and at what point did humour begin to mutate into something darker or more haunting? I actually made the entire album musically first and only added the dialogue afterwards. The way I work is that I name every track very deliberately. Every title has a story behind it. The music follows the title, not the other way around. I usually start with a name and then create the music around it. Once the music was finished, I went through the film and selected lines that fit the story or feeling of each track. I chose dialogue that reinforced the intention behind the music. As for the darker humour, I think that’s just part of my personality. I’ve always had a dark sense of humour and probably always will. So if the comedy turns into something more unsettling, it wasn’t necessarily intentional. I simply chose the lines that felt right and helped tell the story I wanted each track to convey. You write that the album was made during a period when everything felt “stretched—mentally, emotionally, politically.” How do tracks such as “Trauma,” “No Means No,” and “Homeless” reflect that state of mind? Were these pieces tied to specific experiences, or are they more abstract emotional landscapes? At the time I was working in a supermarket while learning Hebrew because I wanted to improve my language skills and eventually get into university. I had a very strict routine. Every day I had a list of things I needed to accomplish: work, make music, learn how to draw, study the language, and keep improving myself. My life was extremely structured. I hardly went out at all. Ironically, my mind was actually very clear during that period. I even stopped smoking for nine months because I wanted that sense of clarity and focus while making the album. Every song on the record was intentional. Even a track like “Homeless” came from a specific experience. It was winter, and I was on a bus heading home from work while it was raining heavily. I saw a homeless man searching through a garbage bin for food. It suddenly hit me that I had a home, food, and basic security, while this man had none of those things. That moment stayed with me. So no, these tracks aren’t abstract emotional landscapes. They always come from something concrete and meaningful. photo by Bouncyduck One of the most interesting ideas in the album is that the Palestinian reality is present without being directly stated. Rather than slogans or explicit references, it emerges through repetition, tension, and a feeling of being trapped in cycles. How conscious was this approach, and do you think music can sometimes communicate political realities more effectively through atmosphere than through direct representation? You’re right, and I’m glad you noticed that. I actually dislike stating things directly. I’m also a filmmaker and animator, and one of the first things you’re taught is: don’t tell—show. I don’t want to give listeners facts or explain everything. I want to create an experience and let them arrive at their own understanding. I have the tools to make people feel something, and for me that’s much more powerful than simply telling them what to think. When someone explains a situation to you, you might understand it intellectually. But when you experience even a small fragment of that feeling yourself, it stays with you. You don’t forget it. That’s why I prefer atmosphere, emotion, and suggestion. It’s my way of communicating through music. Looking across your recent work—from Palestine Is Always War and In the Life of a Palestinian Prisoner to Blue Is the Only Color I See, Hello World Bye World, and now It’s Either Me or My Auntie—there seems to be a shift from overtly documentary and political themes toward more psychological and internal forms of expression. Do you see this latest album as a continuation of those earlier concerns, or does it represent a new chapter in your artistic practice? Actually, It’s Either Me or My Auntie was made before Blue Is the Only Color I See and Hello World Bye World, although it came after Palestine Is Always War. So I don’t really think of it as a shift. It’s more a reflection of the state of mind I was in while making the album. I never approach my work thinking, “Now I’m moving from political themes to psychological themes.” I simply make whatever feels honest at that particular moment. Every record contains a part of me that people don’t normally get to see. That’s really the only constant. I don’t think in terms of artistic chapters. I just create whatever represents me at that point in time. Humour plays a surprisingly important role on this record. The source material is comedic, yet the album often feels anxious, claustrophobic, and emotionally charged. In a context where everyday life can be marked by uncertainty and pressure, what role do absurdity, comedy, and laughter play for you personally? Can humour itself become a form of resistance or survival? Humour plays a huge role in my life. It’s how I communicate difficult truths. I’ve always used comedy as a way of talking about serious things. Life feels absurd to me. I’ve spent years reading Albert Camus and other absurdist and existentialist writers, and they’ve shaped the way I think. Questions about why we live, how we find meaning, and how we deal with suffering have always been important to me. Because of that, I often use humour as a vehicle for difficult emotions and uncomfortable realities. If you approach someone directly with heavy subjects, they might listen, but the impact is different. Humour creates another way in. It makes ideas memorable. It allows people to engage with difficult truths without immediately rejecting them. My music is very personal, and I always try to be honest. I never lie. Sometimes the truth isn’t delivered directly—it comes wrapped in jokes, laughter, or absurdity. People often think I’m just being funny, but the people who know me best understand that my jokes aren’t really jokes. They’re simply another way of telling the truth. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by tszirmay — I was quite impressed with the previous 2024 'Empty' album, as I was expecting something heavy and predictable and it turned out to be neither. Will this follow-up continue in that direction ? Well, we shall find out! Kristoffer handles pretty much everything with a few guests Leo Margarit handling the drum stool chores , and two guitarist invited to play each on one track. From the initial opener 'Rendering', the tectonic symphonism slides in like a needle in an arm, a pronounced melancholia as opposed to metallic noise, the riffs crisp, the mood expansive and imperious. A perfectly opened door to the more revealing 'Nothing Lasts Forever' where the voice is able to traverse the soft and into the extreme, I guess the best description would be 'intensely romantic'. The instrumental edifice swims in passionate despair, with huge dollops of regret and finally, acceptance. Sturdy drumbeats and startled electronics set the stage for some rifferama on the earthy 'Landfill', a foundational crevasse from which Kristoffer's voice rises into a muffled rant, with more than enough gruesome intonations, and effects. Daniel Magdic unleashes a hot guitar solo that spews like molten lava erupting from some shifting tectonic plate. Contrast that eruption with the more grizzled 'The Almosts', a vital track that has a more melodic and even cinematographic, steamrolling along with measured force, the shrouded voice dripping with perspiration and a choral outbreak that shifts along, melodically unswerving. The instrumental segment pounds mercilessly and the apotheosis arrives soon enough to its full conclusion. An 'Intermezzo' is inserted to draw a line in the sand, a tingling guitar with Spanish intonations, lamenting some misty spirit caught between two worlds and unable to find either heaven or hell. Unexpectedly delicious, the way a brief intermission should always be. 'Nothing Stays the Same ' reverts into the lilting melancholia that characterizes the artist's style, and it works because the vocal performance is utterly convincing, pleading and contrite. The expression is both hard and soft, as it blends into an enduring mellotron storm, electric guitars shifting with measured menace, and the angst shattering the will. Staying resolutely in the same mindset, 'The Fields' talk about his Achilles heel, a metallic arrow firmly imbedded in the tendon, where rough riffs and soft voices collide. Thijmem van der Meer's bleeding lead guitar adding colourful trauma, while Leo pumps all the blood out of his kit. Time to mix it up a little with some athletic pyrotechnics, as espoused on the alarming 'Before I Fall Asleep' , the lengthiest track presented here at 6:42, as well as being the most intricate, less reliant on vigor, opting for a more elaborate foundation, what with the organ/bass interplay, the drums more in the background. Then the droning electronics signal a change of pace and heart, the mania seeping in between each power riff and banging beat, the voice now unwavering and the instrumental outro explosive. Nintendo-like pings and pongs take this straight into the pillow-laden cradle. The final dream sequence is the electronics-driven 'Binary', arguably the softest piece here, an ornamental piano doing wonders amid all the layered synths, a fitting symphonic closing to a satisfying album. This final track was my favourite one. I still prefer 'Empty', as it was more attuned to my tastes. 4 tamed urges

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Kayoko Ishu's beautiful voice opens the �lbum, which also lends its title to the entire work, and High-Flying washes over us with all its poetry; Hiromasa's old friend Jiro Inagaki plays the saxophone, and the sophistication of the arrangements reminds me of Luis Alberto Spinetta's A 18' del Sol and Return to Forever in 1972, a group that, with Flora Purim, also tried to reach the sun without getting burned... like Icarus, though both Chick and Hiromasa have fared better.A fusion style, funk yet symphonic, permeates "Screwdriver": a pronounced bassline, jingle-like percussion that instantly transports the listener, and sharply syncopated breaks that, combined with electric guitars, create an atmosphere of relaxed nonchalance. The electric guitar was rarely funkier than on Scramble, and the saxophones, challenging it, refuse to be left behind. Meanwhile, the synthesizer in the background binds everything together, draping it all in a transparent blanket so that it remains audible at all times, while the guitar plays bluesy notes that evolve into the kind of classic jazz-rock riffs that make you move involuntarily.Here, everyone sounds well-oiled and in perfect unison; there is melody, but also improvisation and those jam sessions where Hiromasa's Minimoog, backed by Jun Fukamachi, joins the mix. "Between O&M" might feature harmonies reminiscent of Stanley Clarke on electric bass, but the train the band boards offers no respite; one barely catches a glimpse of the scenery before the next view rushes in (which invites repeated listening later on). Absolutely everyone takes part in this funk odyssey, which at times veers into psychedelic territory.On "Smash", we have the pleasure of hearing Hiromasa play the acoustic piano within his band's electric setting; when he wanted to show off his virtuosity, he certainly did so, while still conveying genuine emotion, something always appreciated. There are so many musical ideas scattered throughout "Straight Flash" that it is hard to believe it lasts just over five minutes; the solos flow one after another, maintaining a style of pure, high-speed, jazz-infused funk that boasts a progressive complexity making it truly admirable.For the finale, "Out of Focus," Kayoko Ishu once again delights us with that ethereal atmosphere, neither Bossa Nova nor Soul, but a fusion of both, as if Burt Bacharach had directed the vocal section. The electric piano serves as a haven in that dark ocean where we float... yet, guided by the music, we are not adrift; instead, we are moving toward a clearly defined destination.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The album was titled By the Red Stream, though it could well have been called a "Summit Reunion", much like the one that brought Astor Piazzolla and Gerry Mulligan together in 1974. A year earlier, pianist and keyboardist Hiromasa Suzuki had joined forces with saxophonist Jiro Inagaki to create pure fusion in the style of Miles Davis, yet infused with Big Band elements (featuring three trombones, three trumpets, and tenor and baritone saxophones) and heavy doses of funk and rock. At times, the sound turned cosmic or took on an Eastern flair reminiscent of John Coltrane, fearlessly embracing atonality while keeping the rhythm firmly on their side. Cacophony aside, they knew exactly how to weave in a new melody whenever the original one went astray.One gets the impression that the modernist spirit of the late 60s and early 70s permeates this recording, a sound that, despite superficial variations, reached audiences across the globe in much the same way. "Warm, Honest and Love" showcases the warmth of the wind section alongside the piano, evoking the orchestrations of Isaac Hayes, while Hiromasa displays his acoustic piano mastery, honed in his trio setting; he stands out not by playing at breakneck speed (though he certainly could), but by creating atmosphere and contributing ideas and emotion in tandem with the double bass and saxophone. This acoustic dynamic contrasts beautifully with a much more experimental electric approach; for instance, on "There Is Not Any War to End the War," the entire wind section plays together in an atonal, highly dissonant fashion, yet they start and stop with precision. Here, the saxophone, in perfect rapport with the electric piano, truly shines, seeming to soar toward the stars or into that other dimension of the Red Sea depicted on the album cover.The music follows the cadences of the title, which is highly evocative, almost a manifesto. And Hiromasa possessed as much jazz sensibility on the piano as he did groove on the keyboard. Jiro Inagaki and the trumpets take the baton, until the big band kicks in again for an apocalyptic finale."Something over the War" unleashes a frenetic race between the electric piano and Yasuo Arakawa's bass; almost imperceptibly, Suzuki constructs a new melody, albeit a jagged one, drawing on the varied tonal colors of the different saxophones, all of them part of that "red stream" known as war, a current against which we all struggle to swim.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — The sudden and cascading beauty of this album has elevated it to the ranks of the most esteemedprogressive rock releases of the 2010s, with a lush and mournful sound that defies tradition andconjures up some of the most heartbreaking melodies to have come out of Anathema. This is, ofcourse, the album 'We're Here Because We're Here', which happens to be the Liverpudlian band's eightstudio release and first studio collection of all-original material since 2003's 'A NaturalDisaster'. This is also where female singer Lee Douglas, sister of drummer John Douglas, joined theband as a full-time member, having previously appeared as a guest on preceding releases. As for thealbum itself, written primarily by Daniel Cavanagh, 'WHBWH' is where Anathema perfected the balancebetween alternative riffs and atmospheric beauty. An album about love and death, an album with asprawling sentimental feel, and one dedicated to melodic discovery - this is precisely where it allcomes together for this band.The ten tracks appearing here vary in length, with a few reaching the seven- or eight-minute mark,adding up to some fifty-eight minutes of stunning art rock. Opener 'Thin Air' sets an intimate,melancholic tone with its sweeping guitars and pulsating percussion, while the beautiful vocalsdeliver a dose of bittersweet heartache. The song 'Summernight Horizon' then introduces a hypnotic,almost angsty riff, set against a vivid piano, while the male and female voices complement eachother gracefully on top. Third track 'Dreaming Light' reverts back to more ambient textures, while'Everything' re-ignites the album's uplifting energy with some gentle riffs. 'Angels Walk Among Us'continues the thread of elevated, quasi-spiritualistic alternative rock, with yet another stunningchorus, while the shorter piece 'Presence' seemingly concludes the first half of the record on acalmer note. 'A Simple Mistake', seventh on the tracklist, then picks up a haunting melodic build-upthat sees Anathema at their most compositionally mature. The sound of this song is exalted andmoving, and the same applies to 'Get Off, Get Out', a song that distantly echoes 'Fear of a BlankPlanet', at least in my ears. The album closes off with two intense and instrumentally peculiarsongs - 'Universal and 'Hindsight', the latter of which is a dreamy, almost symphonic-ladencomposition with ghostly vocals from Lee Douglas.I continue to be amazed by this album. Its sheer beauty is something I cannot comprehend, and eventhough it is a record I do not play so often, every new listen is simply delirious. Out ofeverything I have heard from Anathema, 'We're Here Because We're Here' is their crowningachievement.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — The Brasilian Jazz fusionists are back with another solid album, this one again recorded in the United States (at Capitol Records & Indigo Ranch). It was released by Capitol Records on August 21, 1978. This one was also produced by the same Larry Dunn-Eduardo Del Barrio-Jorge Strunz and Larkin Arnold team that the last album was produced by with the addition of horn specialist Steve Tavaglione also helping out.1. "The Arousing" (2:50) an obvious "intro" song, it's just too Smooth and cinematic for my tastes: sounding more like soundtrack music for some American television show. (4.375/5)2. "Reviviscence" (7:00) flowing directly from the previous "introductory" song without break, I do not like the weak sound and volume coming from Gregg Lee's bass nor the weak/distant sounds coming from Alex Acuna's drums. The rest of the band is fine--up to their usual quality of performance (though they do feel a little rote/uninspired: as if they've played this song a million times and are tired of it). (13.25/15)3. "Mosaico" (7:00) here we get some Stanley Clarke feel from Gregg Lee, and some Chick Corea from Eduardo del Barrio, giving the music a bit of a RTF/Chick Corea sound and feel (which can never be a bad thing). Jorge Strunz even fills some of the song's numerous spaces with some very fine Al Di Meola-like acoustic guitar work (only with nylon stringed guitars as well as steel), which is very impressive, but where the song comes up a bit short is with any kind of cohesive themes or melody lines. Also, I just don't like the Smooth Jazz saxophone lines (and sounds) coming from Steve Tavaglione (which I know were the in-demand sounds of the era due to the popularity and success of artists like David Sanborn, Jay Beckenstein, Najee, and Kenny G). Still, I cannot find total dissatisfaction with anything this well imitative of Chick-Corea-like complexity. (13.25/15)4. "Magewind" (1:34) piano, harp, and full orchestra, sounding like some excellent soundtrack music from a 1950s film. (4.625/5)5. "Crosscountry" (5:24) this one comes across as a kind of combination of Earl Klugh, Bob James, and Spyro Gyra. It's not bad: very well performed (from some challenging charts, I have no doubt), and I don't mind the slips into orchestral Disco palettes--it's rather pretty--but something just feels a bit too pop-oriented. Still, I can't help but rate this one upward for its conglomeration of stellar individual musicianship. (9/10) 6. "Passages" (7:30) there is a problem with the levels of the individual tracks in the mix of this song that bothers me despite the fine performances from all of its musicians. Also, the composition, as admirably complex as it is, lacks enough hooks and melody for me to engage (it uses a bit too much dissonance and atonality for my tastes). In the fifth minute the high strings sustained note bridges the band's leap into a "Birdland"-inspired motif in which Gregg Lee's fretless bass and Eduardo's PolyMoog go a bit crazy (not unlike a Jaco and Jan Hammer duel). (13.25/15)7. "Dreamborne" (1:40) a nice and impressive classical guitar solo from Jorge Strunz. He is definitely a virtuoso: one of the finest players I've ever heard. (4.625/5)8. "Shanti" (4:00) with wordless female vocalese, this Disco-funk tune feels like something from one of those orchestra-enhanced artists who specialized in covering recent pop hits (this one being an Earth, Wind & Fire tune). In the end it sounds like one of the anthemic vehicles that DAVID SANBORN used to gain fame and popularity. (8.875/10) 9. "Horizon's End" (8:18) an interesting four-part tune whose themes are split pretty evenly between the eight minutes. The first is one of those Latin-infused repeating four-chord circle-dance tunes with repeating guitar riff providing the foundation for everyone else to parade over. In the third minute the motif straightens out into something more RTF-like: Power Fusion with lots of flashy soloing helping to fill the numerous pregnant spaces and pauses as well as some awesome Mahavishnu/RTF-like whole-group flurries and runs. At 4:30 there is a long pause of dead silence before Jorge enters with his classical guitar to inject a different kind of Latin flavor with a little guitar-plus-flute interlude before the band suddenly appears in toto a minute later to leap into a speedy five-chord motif over which Steve's flute and Eduardo's electric piano fly along over the racing support crew beneath. The best song on the album--the one that sounds the most like peak quality Third Wave Jazz-Rock Fusion. (18.25/20)Total Time 43:20Where I don't necessarily love the overall feel that this album's music leaves me with, I am in true awe of the amazing musicianship captured in these tracks--including George Del Barrio's amazing orchestral inputs/arrangements. Everyone of these musicians needs to be included in our lists of great musicians for their individual virtuosities. B+/4.5 stars; other than the first two songs, we have here another near-masterpiece of incredibly-well-engineered music from these amazing musicians.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Brasilian band's sophomore album release comes a year after their debut. Recording in Los Angeles with Earth, Wind & Fire's Larry Dunn in the production booth meant the guest appearances of some notable American musicians and some additional orchestration on some of the songs. The album was released by Capitol Records on April 28, 1977.1. "Sky Islands" (6:12) quite good poppy/melodic Smooth Jazz Funk that sounds as if Earth, Wind & Fire had stuck to the wordless choir vocal-instrumental format and palette of their 1975 breakout album, Gratitude. It's infectious and so enjoyable/danceable even if it is at times sounding a little dated and shlocky! Nice reckless-abondon guitar shredding from Jorge Strunze in the fifth minute. (9.75/10)2. "Ancient Source" (4:33) an awesome pop-Jazz tune with a gorgeous, melodic, and very impressive lead vocal from Diane Reeves. The easy-going orchestra-enhanced Latin foundation is sublime. (9.75/10)3. "It Used to Be" (1:14) Eduardo del Barrio's piano solo with flutey synth embedded within. (4.375/5)4. "Pegasus" (4:59) another pop-jazz tune that has a Urszula Dudziak/Michal Urbaniak feel to it as well as some amazing sound clarity due to the advanced electric engineering techniques being taken advantage of. It is definitely founded in Latin/Brasilian traditions, complete with awesome acoustic guitar solo in the second and third minute and two piano tracks in the keyboard solo in the fourth. Lite, rhythmically-engaging, and upbeat, it's a little too 1980s World Music, missing something. (8.875/10)5. "Carnavalito" (4:52) Eduardo's synth-generated pan flutes match the pan flute lines of Steve Tavaglione as the song unfolds like something from early Chick Corea/Return To Forever only more fluffed up with Smooth Jazz sounds and effects (soprano sax, rhythm guitar, occasional near-Disco riffs). Another nice exhibition of lead guitar in the fourth minute as the band stalls beneath with two chords being put on repeat. Synths and horns solo freely as vocal "hey!"s accent the final minute's music as a horn section might. Interesting but a little too schmaltzy to be included in Third Wave fare. (8.75/10)6. "Seraphim (Angel)" (4:47) now we get to something that feels like a cover of a vocal-led Soul pop songonly this one has no vocals, only flutes, synths, hand claps, acoustic guitar, orchestra strings, tenor sax, and exploding funky bass notes/riffs (piano, rhythm guitar, drums, & percussion are less forward, more background/support). Very pretty and soothing in a funky-groovin' way. (8.875/10)7. "Indigo Fire" (1:08) an impressive ANT PHILLIPS-like acoustic guitar duet from Jorge Strunz. (4.875/5)8. "Triste" (6:51) another gorgeous Smooth Jazz Funk sound palette that sounds like instrumental EW&F, only with the support of orchestra strings and more Jazzy solo options from soprano sax, electric piano, and "dirty" electric guitar. GREAT Smooth Jazz base, though. (13.333/15)9. "Pescador (Fisherman)" (1:05) the percussionists solo song (with inclusion of Eduardo's odd squeaky synth sounds). (4.375/5)Total Time 34:32B+/4.5 stars; a near-masterpiece of wonderfully-rich Smooth Jazz. Really enjoyable music. Highly recommended if you want to create the ambiance of a breezy Caribbean island beach cabana scene.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A debut record from a band of West Coast (California) musicians that was recorded and mixed at Hollywood Sound in Los Angeles in July of 1976 and then released by Capitol Records later in the year.A1. "Guanacaste" (6:31) a song that seems to say "Disco is here so you might as well enjoy it--in the instrumental form as well". The band produces a very nice, tight weave of the entire ensemble with catchy, if pedestrian, melodies and great engineering and production. (8.875/10)A2. "Coastin"' (4:42) bass, drums, novelty rubber duck synth notes, female vocalese, clavinet, guitars and saxophone are all added, almost one at a time, until a break at 1:40. When the band returns their fun-funky motif is used to support a searing electric guitar solo from Jorge Strunz (the same Costa Rican guitarist who would, in the 1980s, become one half of the acoustic guitar duo that would become one of the globe's most popular/famous World Music bands, Strunz & Farah). I like this unusual song. (9/10)A3. "Exaltation" (6:52) there are some really great parts to this (like the awesome bass, rhythm guitar, and percussion lines in the fourth and fifth minutes) but there area also some passages that really drag (like the third minute). I like the pairing of the synth and female vocalese in the final minute to create a kind of Michal Urbaniak-Ursula Dudziak effect. (13.125/15)B1. "Synesthesia" (7:45) the only song the album that is attributed to only one composer (Jorge Strunz), the guitarist is prominent but gives up the lead shine to his sax, electric piano player, and trombonist in lieu of himself, which is admirable, and Steve Tavaglinoe, Eduardo Del Barrio, and Raoul De Souza, respectively, do not disappoint. In the sixth minute Jorge finally takes his turn, supplying a solo that reminds me quite a bit of Cervello and Nova lead guitar phenom Corrado Rustici, which is quite impressive. It's a fine song; if only it had more hooks and earworms. (13.25/15)B2. "Out Of The Blue" (4:46) a more laid-back Smooth Jazz piece of Funk Lite that sounds as if it could have come from Bob James's production studio or the Laws family: finely crafted, extremely well performed and engineered, rolling the listener through some great hooks that have become staples for the Pop Jazz world. (9/10)B3. "El Juguete" (8:31) the album's final song has an awesome racehorse start straight out of the gate: cruising along until the band has to reign things in with a bridge to show off its whole band unity and precision, flute and guitar mirroring one another in the lightning fast melody line that ends the long bridge. At this point the band settles into a slow tempo as trombonist Raoul De Souza takes the lead but then about 15 seconds into his solo the band ramps up into fifth gear with bass, percussion, drums, and electric piano really flying along beneath Raoul's 'bone! At 3:30 there is a tag to hand off the lead to Steve Tavaglione and his flute as the rest of the band retools and gradually regains its high-speed momentum. This is awesome! So fun! So rollicking and carefree! It's almost like being on a train or rollercoaster! And Steve is an awesome flutist! In the sixth minute the band slows things down again to a trot while Jorge solos frenetically with a mean distorted guitar tone. Again the band slowly rebuilds its tempo to breakneck speed and full breadth of participation from everybody on board until they bring the party to a raucous close together at the end. My favorite song on the album--one that deserves the highest praise for its representation of top quality Third Wave Jazz-Rock Fusion. (19.125/20)Total Time: 38:40A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of mostly high quality Third Wave Jazz-Rock Fusion.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 978Gentle Giant was a British prog band that was formed in London and that was active until 1980. Gentle Giant was formed of a blues based and later psychedelic band named Simon Dupree & The Big Sound, in 1970. It featured the multi-instrumental Shulman brothers Derek, Ray and Phil. They joined with the guitarist Gary Green, the keyboardist Kerry Minnear and several drummers Martin Smith, Malcolm Mortimore and the most consistent of all John Weathers. Gentle Giant was one of the most innovative and technically complex bands of the British progressive rock movement of the 70's. Although they never achieved the commercial success of bands like Pink Floyd or Genesis and having had a short life, they are now considered a gem of the genre for their compositional rigor, a true paradigmatic prog band."Prologue" is a double live album of Gentle Giant that was released in 2003. Originally, this material circulated only as a bootleg. The recordings are from two distinct performances in the 70's: Munster, Germany on April 5, 1974. It fills the entire first disc and the first three tracks of the second. Philadelphia, USA on October 10, 1975. It occupies the final four tracks of the second disc. The repertoire is focused on the band's golden era. It has tracks from "Gentle Giant", "Acquiring The Taste", "Three Friends", "Octopus", "In A Glass House", "The Power And The Glory" and "Free Hand". "Prologue" has fourteen tracks. "The Runaway" and "Experience" were originally released on "In A Glass House". "The Runaway" has rich varieties of styles and textures, melodic, complex and creative. It's a great track, one of the best by the band. "Experience" is inventive with a complex structure. It's an example of the band's medieval complex sound. It also has other varied forms of music. It's rich with wonderful vocal harmonies. "Prologue" was originally released on "Three Friends". "Prologue", as its name indicates, gave its name to this live album. It progresses nicely with great performances especially with strong keyboard riffs and an excellent bass line. "Funny Ways" was originally released on "Gentle Giant". It's a mellow track with a nice exploration of several instruments, classic and acoustic, and electric too. It's relatively complex, a perfect example of their unique sound. "Knots" and "The Advent Of Panurge" were originally released on "Octopus". "Knots" is one of their most complex and intricate tracks. It's an avant-garde track exploring a cappella vocal style. It's a perfect example of the great vocal work of this band. "The Advent Of Panurge" is full of energy, varied melodies and different singing styles. It's apparently chaotic where all instruments seem to be played in different directions. But, it has an excellent harmony. "Nothing At All" was originally released on "Gentle Giant". It begins as a soft and nice acoustic ballad with melancholic harmonies, but that grows as a hard and heavy rock track. It's one of the most interesting tracks by the band. "Plain Truth" was originally released on "Acquiring The Taste". It's a solid rock track with the typical Gentle Giant's sound with good vocal harmonies. It's an accessible track without great complexity and more traditional. It's less typical than usual. "In A Glass House" was originally released on "In A Glass House". It's excellent with great harmony. The chorus is of superior quality. It has a hard rock section with a memorable guitar riff. This is also an amazing track. "School Days" was originally released on "Three Friends". It's nice with experimental vocals and musical passages. It has the use of several instruments at the same time. It also has beautiful piano work, one of the best performances by Kerry Minnear. Phil Shulman sings wonderfully. It's also one of his best vocal moments. "Intro/Cogs In Cogs" was originally released on "The Power And The Glory". It's another excellent track with complex multi-part vocal harmonies. It has an intricate orchestral arrangement. "Excerpts From Octopus", as its name indicates, has excerpts that were originally released on "Octopus". It includes significant parts and solos based on five songs from the original album: "The Boys In The Band", "Raconteur Troubadour", "Dog's Life", "Knots" and "The Advent Of Panurge". The medley is amazing, one of the greatest testaments to Gentle Giant's musical genius and technical virtuosity on stage. "So Sincere" was originally released on "The Power And The Glory". It's a complex and dissonant track. It's experimental and avant-garde with jazz influences. It has certain nonsense, a rather exquisite song. "Free Hand" was originally released on "Free Hand". It's an elaborate and complex track. It's a traditional Gentle Giant's track with some dissonant parts and with constant changes of rhythm and tempo, in the Gentle Giant's style.Conclusion: As I mentioned above, "Prologue" is an "official bootleg" live album from Gentle Giant, as happened with some other live albums released by the band. At this moment it comes to my mind two: "Interview In Concert" and "King Alfred's College Winchester". From what I remember, I own these two live albums too, "Prologue" is probably the one that has a better sound. I agree with Badabec. There is just one track that has a really bad sound quality: "School Days". Of the others, the sound is acceptable or even good. And the sound quality is the only reason I don't give it 4 stars. The track list is excellent and is well representative of the band, and the performance is amazing too. So, 3 stars.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: Review by Matti — This is the debut album of the Swiss harp-playing artist often categorized as New Age. Seemingly it has been released internationally only in the 2-CD set The Trilogy, which I purchased in 1992 soon after discovering Vollenweider's charming music from library. The album info here misses the track titles, but perhaps they weren't in the original LP then. The Trilogy in turn misses several parts of the suite.The main difference to his later works is the greater amount of guitars, both electric and acoustic. Also I feel, despite the "suite" form, that these highly melodic pieces are more solidly standing as individual compositions whereas many albums usually proceed in a conceptual, voyage-like continuity, where picking up single tracks is quite irrelevant. This is definitely not to say that this suite would miss continuity. On the opening piece 'The Shepherd' (I) Andreas plays harp, ocarina, guitar and soprano sax, creating a piece full of atmosphere, colour and progressivity. 'The Gate Within the Gate' (II) builds from it with a bigger combo of musicians. Max L�sser's electric guitar and the strong rhythm section guarantee the emotional increase.'Her Cat Dance' (IV) features the light, jazzy groove typical for the later output. 'The Letter' (V) is a brief and classically oriented solo piano piece, followed seamlessly by 'Little Boy and the Mirror' (VI) where soprano sax and synths carry the lighthearted melody. There's a hint of Pekka Pohjola or Bj�rn J:son Lindh. 'A Walk With My Father' (VII) is starring Andreas' father on church organ, joined later by Andreas' ocarina. Such a profound depth in this piece. 'Summer Rain' (VIII) is a tiny, light jazz piece highlighting piano and electric guitar. A bit like Pat Metheny. 'Desert in the Horglass' (no numbering, possibly not on the original LP) is a serene, 51-second track for harp, soprano sax, alto flute - and cello which makes me think of the New Agey music of David Darling. This piece ends the version of "The Art Suite" heard on The Trilogy. My apologies for reviewing an album on basis of an incomplete listening experience, but it deserves being revisited nevertheless. Any friend of Vollenweider's personal music would be fortunate if coming across this apparently rare album.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Though Caldera recorded most of their albums in LA, they were a NYC band, filled with members fromall over Latin America and the US. Developing a torrid fusion between Jazz-rock, jazz-funk, Latinjazz , Caldera was a typical product of its era, somewhere between Return To Forever and (to alesser extent) Weather Report, but with added horns. However, the album's sleeve might be a tadmisleading, as you won't find much African in the music. The Latin side doesn't translate much in aSantana world, though. Their music is almost all instrumental,; though there are some appearance ofa female singerThe musical excellence of every band member at their respective instruments was even more impressiveand enhanced by clever songwriting that sometimes approached climates close to progressive rock.Caldera's compositions sometimes reached breakneck speeds, much like RTF, not only by the guitaristStrunz, but also by Del Barrio's choice of the then-modern synths that were more Zawinul's type thanCorea's. Odd thing is that the wind instruments of Tavaglione and De Souza softened the tone andgave it a "soul-ier" feel.With a track like Coastin', one can think of HH's HH (Head Hunters) aswell.Complex, while somewhat relaxing, it's a bit of a headscratcher as to why Caldera"s album flew underthe radar of most aficionados, while the inferior Spiro Gyra attracted much more attention.

Seraphim is probably the album's weaker moment, though, again drowned in string arrangements.Nevertheless, if you manage to ignore those "flaws" (orchestrations and vocals), the band is back with its original brilliance and flawless tightness and progressive climates.

items.body: Review by SilverLight59 — Returned to the Earth's fifth studio release, Stalagmite Steeple is a heavy, dark, yet gorgeous concept album. Rising up from the lingering shadows of the Covid-19 pandemic, the story traces an elderly couple separated during lockdown; the wife passes away alone in a care facility, while corporate billing predictably continues uninterrupted. Rather than exploding in aggressive rage, Returned to the Earth channels this injustice into a quiet but intense, tragic beautiful piece of art rock.Looking at the album cover, we see that the tone of the album is aptly captured in its foreboding atmosphere and presentation. Emphasizing the album title's imagery, the artwork mirrors the bleak, slow-evolving nature of a stalagmite, a structure built drop by drop over vast stretches of time, isolated in the dark. This serving as a perfect parallel companion piece to the lyrical concepts inside. It's a warning to the listener that what lies within is an exploration of the abyss, lacking bright colors but rich in deep, shadowed contrast, if we dare explore there.My first introduction to Returned to the Earth was their preceding album Fall of the Watcher. This came across as melodic and polished neo-prog, but it still maintained an adjacency to mainstream art pop structures making it quite accessible. Stalagmite Steeple on the other hand, shifts the paradigm entirely. It is noticeably more low-key, heavily melancholic, and unhurried than its predecessor. The album abandons any residual desire to please radio formulas, steering entirely into a unified, esoterically somber atmosphere. Where the previous record felt like a collection of beautifully produced, individual statements, this new one winds out as a single, unified journey that takes considerable effort to fully absorb. In short, if you are hoping for Fall of the Watcher part two, you may be disappointed.That being said, Returned to the Earth is quietly building a body of work that is weaving atmospheric musical landscapes and lyrical tapestries that reach the listeners emotions and psyche. Led by singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist Robin Peachey, alongside Paul Johnston and Steve Peachey, the band is creating its own unique space in the prog universe. Notably, with each release, they have been moving more and more to reject hyper-technical, "mile a minute" instrumental showmanship in favor of spacious, slow-burning compositions allowed to breathe and unfold at an organic pace. With Stalagmite Steeple, this is truer than ever. If this is your cup of tea, this will satisfy your expectations in a big way. So let's take a brief look at the tracks.1. Dark Morality (7:19)The album opens with probably its most accessible track, its flagship single, perfectly setting the slow, plodding thematic tone that will largely be a precursor for much of the album and the songs within. Driven by a deliberate, descending chord progression and a heavy, chugging bass line, the song allows Peachey's warm, clean vocals to come to the fore and really shine. The guitar work for the final couple minutes slowly grows in intensity with a bit of a Porcupine Tree groove to it. There is an expectation for it to totally break loose, but instead it fades out which is a bit of disappointment, but a fine track nonetheless. One other minor complaint, the first thirty to forty seconds of this track is entirely inaudible, which I find to be very annoying. (8.5/10)2. The Final Time (5:00)A profoundly mournful ballad addressing the literal moment the album's subject passes away, isolated from her family. Sorrowful orchestration underpins the track, again with gradual build up, then a full drop off in pace, and finally a soaring, crying guitar solo cuts underneath the mix to articulate the grief being painted. (8/10)3. Stalagmite Steeple (9:58)The title cut and the near-ten-minute centerpiece. This opens with an unhurried, hypnotic, cyclical piano line and low key lyrics. At the 2:30 mark, big guitar line changes the mood. While overall the track builds with restraint, the layering expressive guitars and a floating melody instrumental section elevates the emotion. About midway the music strips back down to the opening piano and lyric motif. As has been mentioned by others, there is similarity with the style of Tim Bowness lyrically, and indirectly, Steven Wilson musically here. The final two minutes begin once again to escalate the intensity. The structure is nice, but once again there is the thought that it may break open, but restraint is the coda here, as this one also fades out to finish it off. (8.25/10)4. Meaningless to Worth (6:09)Acting as the thematic pivot, this track transitions from the couple's personal perspective to the broader social failures of the pandemic era. It is incredibly subdued and reserved for the first two minutes, then drums and synth wash enters raising the tone, at three minute guitars enter. At four minutes the full rhythm section finally lands, and builds up a nice intensity which plays out to the end. (8.5/10)5. Die for Me (9:09)The second longest track. Starts with a wobbling synth wash. Yet another slow build, but the vocal quickly lifts this track up. Guitars come in underneath and this starts to become the most dynamic and structurally propelled track on the record. There is a calming pause midway which rebuilds the track and introduces an even busier, electronic rhythm track that breaks up the album's prevailing understated essence, culminating in a powerful, shuddering guitar solo that vents genuine anger at the institutional systems that failed society. This one actually opens up at the end and builds to a big finale we have been waiting for. (9.75/10)6. The Raging Sea (5:36)The album closes not with a continuation of the dramatic storm, an intense final statement, but rather with a velvety, calming melody meant to offer a sense of resolution. The ebb and flow of the music featuring a lovely guitar lead and warm bass lines mimicking the tides, pointing toward an ideal of natural peace where humanity must eventually return after trauma. The emotional floating vocal melodies over the atmospheric soundscape closes out the album with an overarching sense of resolution and hope. A very nice and accessible track for the finish. (9.5/10)So, what is the final takeaway at the end of the day? While Stalagmite Steeple is a triumph of tasteful atmosphere, pristine production, and emotional resonance, a realistic critique must note what some may see as its limitations. Because the band is so wholly committed to a deeply meditative low-key mood, the album can occasionally feel restrictive in its expression . Listeners who crave shifting time signatures, aggressive rock bombast, or instant melodic payoffs may find themselves waiting for a musical explosion that never arrives. The songs intentionally build beautiful foundations but sometimes refuse to "dress" them with standard rock climaxes. It requires a measure of patience and the right, introspective headspace to fully appreciate the soundscapes being developed. Ultimately, I really like what is going on herein, and I am of the opinion that Stalagmite Steeple is a bold progression for the band as it doesn't rest on being an extension of their last album, but will stand alone as a unique and singular milestone. It is totally different, and as such, a brave, carefully constructed, and elegant exploration of human grief. Perhaps not the happiest of subjects, but a worthy one given the times that we live in. For those willing to slow down and unplug from the fast-paced and largely insensitive world we are all part of, and submerge themselves in its reflective lyrical depths and methodical musical expressions, it functions not as a depressive wallowing in grief, but in the end, a nurturing, healing, uplifting message of reconciliation. You may need to be in the right mind set to take this one in, but it is well worth the effort. 4 deeply reflective stars.

items.body: Review by XixoTheRock — Spinetta...the thousand sounds man, he is distinctive for his long standing tradition of startingbands, releasing some masterpieces then ditching them and starting a new one, this was the case forInvisible, chronologically, Invisible is his fourth band after the collapse of Pescado rabioso(which had practically, by the release of Artaud, become his solo project). Therefore, this, asInvisible's debut album, will have a somewhat transitional and tense sound, almost as if the new andold band identities were playing tug of war, this, which in theory, should harm the record, actuallystrengthens it's quality, since it creates an organic, vivid mix of Pescado rabioso's folk,acoustic, surreal and sensitive textures with the symphonic, grandiose, experimental and jazzy soundof Invisible...this is a recipe for a listen that is engaging in every possible way, filled withlittle details that require time to fully digest and understand fully, therefore, this is alsoincredibly relistenable.(It's absolutely worth noting that, Invisible is a supergroup just as ELP was, this will influencetheir releases significantly as they're much more intricate and technical than other Spinettarecords)One of the things that separates this record from other Spinetta releases, is it's accessibility,not much of his music is quite accesible and easy for the casual listener (even as he had hits andfame, most of his music remained too Avant Garde for the general public), this would be inherited byInvisible's final record "El jardín de los presentes" 2 years later. Some of the compositions arequite art pop just like Alan Parsons! The opening track "Jugo de lúcuma" comes to mind regardingthis, the clean guitar tones, sensible playing style, and the balance and dynamics betweeninstruments create textures that can be felt like landscapes that shift each second, just like aplacid, deep sleep that induces you in a beautiful, whimsical dream.The strongest feat of the record is the musicianship, as mentioned above, this is a supergroup, eachmember knows when to attack, paint and when to step back, therefore the compositions are not bloatedand each note can be heard crystal clear, it's a ship that's democratically run and sails through aglowing ocean, you can feel the angle the pick plays the strings and the flick of the wrist thedrummer makes each bea..their chemistry is quite organic and flows naturally, you can tell theywere all quite disciplined on their playing but also.paid attention to delivering emotion, each onesynchronized perfectly with the other.I can't say much about the compositions that hasn't already been said, after all it's Spinetta whowe're talking about. But I will say some things regardless of that, since I do have quite some stuffto tell you, about the way this music feels.The compositions are creative and sensitive! You can feel as if you were there, sitting on a field,during a starry evening in the argentinian Pampa. The music is sensitive, chill and playful, almostlike a beloved childhood memory, Spinetta was a poet before he was a musician, so the music alsotells a story even if the lyrics are absent, what better example than "Azafata del tren fantasma"?It really captures the essence of the poem! It has influences of jazz fusion but they're not overlyon your face, the influences are pretty balanced which highlights the creativity of the compositionsand the uniqueness of it's sound, and since it's a transitional record, it also has that cutesurreal Artaud vibe to it! Can't say much more, Spinetta is just a genius composing.The lyrics are narrative, surreal and personal, contrasting Artaud's dark, gritty and angst filledlyrics, these are rather playful and even optimistic, a complete shift in attitude, nonetheless,they're just as poetic and introspective as Artaud's. The thing that is most enjoyable about theselyrics are the way they tell stories, in a Realismo mágico (Magical realism) Cortázar way, quiteLatin American! Lovers of that literature style will love these!Amazing production, balanced, crystal clear...Overall, it's a record that's worth every single second and dollar if you get to buy it! A uniqueexperience that everyone should feel at least once in their lives.

Yesterdays tooks some solid tracks from the first two albums, Yes & Time and a Word, and threw in America from the Fragile Sessions, and Dear Father- a B-side from Time and a Word.It was a good introduction for the fans that had their classic LP's The Yes Album, Fragile and CTTE. It answered the question, Do I buy Tales and Relayer now? or do i go back further and discover some good earlier material?Decisions decisions, So I bought Yesterdays, then became intrigued and bought Time and a Word, and had to order the original Yes debut. Later went for the Relayer and solo albums.So, if you don't have the first two Yes releases, you can get this and get a real taste of the tht era of Yes and be rewarded with the inclusion of America.Recommendation:Bottom line: This is for completists, unless you're also completing your Roger Dean art collection- these songs can all be had on the reissues of the first two Yes LPs/CDs.and Fragile.Final Sentimental Comment: Sometimes I do listen to this specific CD (well, the MP3 version) because of my memories of the sequencing of the music, that's part of the orginal listening experience I guess.

items.body: The opening of “You Only Live Twice” is one of the most famous John Barry ever wrote: violins dropping two octaves in a run that sounds Japanese but is pure Western scale. He wrote it for the fifth Bond film in 1967, Leslie Bricusse wrote the words, and Nancy Sinatra sang it at CTS Studios in London over a 60-piece orchestra. The melancholy French horn line underneath it was Barry’s too, though he borrowed that from a Tcherepnin piano concerto. London-based The Lo-Tones turn that theme into dub reggae, shrinking the 60-piece score to a small session on brass and keys with the bass sitting heavy underneath. Behind it are Felix Howard, one of British pop’s most established songwriters, who co-wrote the Sugababes’ breakthrough “Overload” and has written for Amy Winehouse, Sia and Kylie Minogue before moving into A&R, now heading it up at Kassner Music, and Tim Hutton, a multi-instrumentalist who has played with the Prodigy, Groove Armada and Above & Beyond since he came up through the anarcho-punk bands The Mob and Zounds on Crass Records. Nick Manasseh mixes it, pulling instruments out until the sub-bass does most of the work: he built his first sound system in 1985 and cut “Seventh Seal”, widely called the first UK Steppers record, three years later. Lovelle, a south-east London singer trained at the Mick Jagger Centre and Sylvia Young, sings Sinatra’s old part low and close to the groove. Manasseh also runs off a full dub version, dropping the vocal and letting the bass and echo carry the track on their own. Stream and listen to “You Only Live Twice” HERE The post Daily Discovery: The Lo-Tones – You Only Live Twice (feat. Lovelle) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Caught between Ruins and dreams Shadow and light Fall from the skies in your eyes A bellow is the raw announcement of need, the body turning pressure into sound. A bellows is need made mechanical, disciplined into rhythm: expand, contract, receive, surrender. Its wisdom lies in reciprocity. Nothing is filled without some neighboring chamber giving way; breath becomes possible through alternating loss. Stranger still, one modest instrument may animate an entire organ, feeding many pipes from a single lung. The image flatters neither independence nor abundance. It suggests that vitality is borrowed, transferred, and timed. What seems like emptiness may be preparation, and what sounds like grandeur may begin in one hidden fold of air. Brittany Bindrim’s new single Bellow places the song between those meanings, where anguish becomes propulsion and intimacy begins as an exchange of damaged parts. The result is dreamy, driving darkwave with warmth in its bloodstream, a song about repair that leaves every seam visible. A steady electronic pulse carries spacious synths and Bindrim’s ethereal vocal, which seems suspended above the beat while remaining closely tied to its forward motion. The arrangement has the buoyancy of a nocturnal drive and the emotional exposure of a confession made before certainty has arrived. Where the album burned, this one breathes, opening a wider chamber around Bindrim’s voice without diluting the tension. Even its brightness has edges, as though tenderness has entered the room without being asked to tidy it. The lyrics imagine two wounded people recognizing corresponding absences in one another. Broken pieces become points of contact; pain becomes a shared language that can be revised rather than merely endured. Bindrim leaves the identity of “we” open enough to contain lovers, collaborators, audiences, or an entire scene held together by mutual rescue. Love, in this conception, offers no return to an untouched original. It produces a new form whose strength depends upon remembering exactly where it fractured. “Bellow lives in dualities — shadow and light, ruins and dreams — until the halves finally fit,” Bindrim says. “The broken parts aren’t flaws to hide; they’re the exact shapes that let us lock into each other. Reassembly isn’t restoration. What comes back is greater than what broke.” The accompanying video places Bindrim inside a mirror-world governed by delay. Her ghosted double follows a breath behind, making each gesture appear divided between action and memory, while the editing locks bodily movement to the song’s measured drive. Doubling becomes less an effect than a visual argument: every self contains its afterimage, every present bears the outline of what preceded it. Watch below: Call Bellow a love song, though Bindrim’s version comes with splinters, sutures, and exposed joins. Its romance lies in reciprocity, in the quiet knowledge that one person may breathe for another until both can stand. Listen to Bellow below and order the single here. items.body: Stiff as a board, light as a feather You held me up forever I should really let go A chunk of my heart and soul Portland post-punk band Darkswoon return with a high-octane remix of “Thread,” the lead single from their fourth LP Antivenom. The remix hails from renowned New York City DJ, producer, musician, and engineer Hi-Fi Hillary, aka Hillary Johnson, head of Kale Shelter Studios. While the original version of “Thread” is a powerful, yet melancholic guitar-driven anthem on love and loss, the remix kicks the song into overdrive, replacing Darkswoon’s shoegaze-inspired guitars with bubbling synth pads and injecting the song’s steady beat with electronic sound and fury. Despite this, vocalist Jana Cushman’s deeply warm and honest vocals add intimacy and vulnerability to the track. As such, the remix is perfect for both the dance floor as well as a long, meditative sunset drive. Darkswoon and Johnson first met during the pandemic as guests on Johnson’s Kale Shelter Twitch streaming series, spotlighting veganism in the underground music scene. Johnson’s many credits over the years include recording/engineering work for bands such as Bootblacks, Liste Noire, Second Still, Angels of Light, Autodrone, My Favorite, and Bell Hollow, the latter of which she also played live keyboards with. She has also recently remixed tracks by Astari Nite, Black Rose Burning, Frenchy and the Punk, IKON, and The Long Losts and has upcoming remixes scheduled with Negative Agent, and The Harrow. She will also be appearing as part of 2026’s Murder of Crows DJ Lineup. Proceeds for this remix will be donated to Animal Aid PDX, a no-kill animal shelter where Cushman has been volunteering at for thirteen years. Be sure to check them out if you live in the area. Otherwise, listen to the track below and stay tuned for a new split 7” release from Darkswoon and Altar Girl to come later in 2026. items.body: I’ve been a ball of fire in your arms desireAnd I’ve been wondering, where it is you’re hiding Gene Loves Jezebel will celebrate the 40th anniversary of their breakthrough third studio album, Discover, with a newly remastered and expanded double-LP reissue arriving July 24 through Beggars Banquet. The collection pairs the original 10-song album with Glad To Be Alive, a concert recording captured in Nottingham in 1986, included as a bonus LP with initial copies of Discover. The live set returns to vinyl here for the first time since that original pressing, while an expanded digital edition will present the complete 17-song performance. The label has offered an early preview with “Desire — Live in Nottingham,” a particularly charged performance of the single that became Gene Loves Jezebel’s calling card. James Stevenson’s familiar guitar introduction quickly gives way to a faster, rougher reading, with Jay and Michael Aston trading and tangling their voices over the band’s relentless momentum. Listen to “Desire — Live in Nottingham” here. And watch the official music video for Desire below: Originally released in 1986, Discover found the Welsh band Gene Loves Jezebel widening their reach of the gothic rock and post-punk heard across Promise and Immigrant. Chiming guitars, forceful rhythms and the Aston twins’ competing voices gave the record a sharper melodic profile, carrying the band from the independent underground toward an international audience. “Desire (Come and Get It)” stood at the center of that advance, joined by “Heartache,” “Sweetest Thing,” “Over the Rooftops” and “Beyond Doubt.” The record retained the tension and theatricality of the band’s earlier work while opening the songs into larger, increasingly direct forms. “This is the album where it all came together for me as a singer & a songwriter,” Jay Aston says. “I discovered myself.” Michael Aston adds: “Feelings with no ceilings, and the thinnest things are a joy forever.” The Aston twins began making music together in 1980, initially working as Slav Arian with guitarist Ian Hudson and a drum machine. Raised in Porthcawl, South Wales, they relocated to London the following year, where the project developed into Gene Loves Jezebel and signed with Beggars Banquet imprint Situation Two. The anniversary edition has been remastered by Henry Rudkins and will be issued on double black vinyl with updated artwork. The first 200 orders placed through the Beggars Banquet store and Bandcamp will include two postcards signed by Jay and Michael Aston, while supplies last. Discover/Glad To Be Alive: 40th Anniversary Expanded Edition arrives July 24 through Beggars Banquet. Pre-order the release here.
