items.body:
Mad hype on this one; the second solo LP by Princ€ss member + Maria Somerville collaborator Finn Carraher McDonald aka Nashpaints , soon to be a collectors thing, big one if you’re into Escho, Cindy Lee, MBV, Jessica Pratt, 4AD, Panda Bear.

There's nostalgia and there's Nostalgia, right? If you survey the output of labels like Escho and 15 love, home to ML Buch, Fine and Snuggle, you'll know that although they play fast and loose with their influences (from Fleetwood Mac to The Sundays to the Happy Mondays), they also augment their sound with so many creative elements that it's like a gust of fresh air across a weathered Northern European plain. Nashpaints has already been spotted wandering the fringes with "avant-pop supergroup" Princ€ss and is a long-time collaborator of Somerville; so it's easy to see why there's no shortage of interest surrounding 'Everyone Good Is Called Molly’. Thankfully, it delivers.

It's one of those records that settles in a historical/cultural no-place, drawing from '50s girl group pop, classic shoegaze, 20th century minimalism, outsider rawk and Phil Spector- not so much a fusion of unrelated ingredients; more the work of a keen listener. McDonald charts a tumultuous relationship between noise and harmony, drawing through lines that pass from The Kinks and the Ronettes to Kevin Shields, Panda Bear and Deerhunter. His second album is pop music, of a sort, and it might also be as tapped into the ha*ntl*gical main vein as Burial's 'Untrue', but it's also endlessly creative, breaking down its influences and rebuilding them as it goes. 

Opener 'Molly' sounds as if it was part of the same thought process that led to Visible Cloaks' 2017 milestone 'Reassemblage', all synth-mallet sounds x swirling nu-age atmospheres. Trapping his ideas in ferric grot, he avoids the cleanness that usually accompanies the sound, accumulating white noise and adding hoarse, black metal-influenced rasps for good measure. Before we've had a chance to gather our thoughts, '23' sets the standard for the rest of the record, playing McDonald's falsetto against chiming, vibrato-laced guitar riffs, percussive outbursts and an omnipresent hiss. McDonald's skill is in finding a way to retain a structured song backbone while fucking with the trimmings: 'The Giver', for example, dissects 50s percussion and reassembles it into a shuffle, while 'Stretching' arguably does the SP-202 waltz groove better than Panda Bear.

When the tone shifts on 'Boyfriend First', replacing the Spector-like trebly guitars with a Shields-esque distorted shimmer, Nashpaints’ careful use of space (and how it impacts harmony), keeps us on track. The warped new age elements that introduce the album eventually re-emerge on the second side and don't sound out of place, cushioning multi-tracked vocals on the ecstatic 'Burning' and washing out his romantic turn on 'Lost Dog', an anachronistic moment that'll surely have many swooning. 

Cop while you can cop.

items.body:
Brazil’s premiere guess-again specialists Lugar Alto have been threatening to unleash this one for a while and here it finally is; compiled by the goat GG Albuquerque and mixed by label enigma Akira Umeda, “My Life is a Movie and In It I Am the Villain” is a compendium of signature DJ drops and idents used in soundsystems from Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo going back to the 1980's and right up to the present day - a genuinely synapse-popping madness that maps the constant evolution of the most vibrant and forward-facing soundsystem cultures of our time...

If you've spent any time with Brazilian funk, you'll know the sonorous intros - always larger-than-life, tongue-in-cheek, fluoro-flavoured - almost as important as the songs themselves. You don't have to understand Portuguese to get the message, either; the cacophony of pitch-wonked vocal stims, familiar samples, pop culture references and cheapo effects is borderless in its appeal, a core component of contemporary funk that's just as important as the syncopated tamborzão beat itself. We've copped tracks that are entirely reliant on the "carimbos" (literally "stamps") and "vinhetas" (intros) so we were hoping someone would put together something like this. And Lugar Alto - the Brazilian imprint responsible for releasing those essential DJ Ramon Successo LPs and that shocking Djalma Corrêa anthology - have taken the most impressive approach imaginable, tasking fount of all knowledge and journalist GG Albuquerque (last seen putting together that sick MÉDIO GRAVE tape for Nyege Nyege Tapes) with compiling something from a genuine street's-eye perspective.

The mix tells a non-linear, multi-dimensional story of Brazilian sound system culture, using DJ drops, stage calls, adverts, cheeky samples and explosive intros made between the 1980s and 2025. It takes us from the point where local sounds collided with funk, freestyle, electro and Miami bass in the wake of 'Planet Rock’ to the moment the scene eventually evolved into the splintered landscape of bruxaria, ritmado, brega and other sounds that we can interface with today via TikTok and Insta. It's a dense, fittingly psychedelic and suitably impertinent mosaic of references, in-jokes and mind-tickling sonics that's seemingly without beginning or end, a time-fluxing braindump of laugh tracks and aborted rhythmic snaps that's best compared to being airlifted into a Rio street party after being shot with medical-grade ketamine. Within a matter of seconds we get John Williams' 'Star Wars' intro followed by a Portuguese Darth Vader voice and a barrage of buzzing "tuin" effects - and it just gets madder and more frenetic from there.

A sort of heatsick parallel narrative to decades of British pirate radio culture, 'Minha Vida...' Is an incredible artefact of a movement that defies easy categorisation, a multi-coloured collage of sounds, humour and idiosyncratic energy that's driven the sound since the very beginning. You can take the boom-cha-cha boom-cha-cha beat, but you can't even begin to mimic the sheer gusto.

items.body:
The second ever public performance by Nurse With Wound, captured on tape in 1984 and held in Steven Stapleton's archive across the four decades since, now available on a vinyl edition for the first time - every copy painted by hand, edition of 300.

You get the measure of this one with Steven Stapleton’s assertion that this was less a gig and more a “series of confrontations with audiences who often had no idea what they were watching.” which is basically everything we hope for watching pretty much anything.

It belongs to a moment when Stapleton, working alongside collaborators including David Tibet, Andrew McKenzie of The Hafler Trio, and a rotating cast of percussionists and string players, was carrying NWW briefly out of the studio. The performance moves through the territory NWW had been mapping across Homotopy to Marie and Nature Unveiled: long passages of pre-recorded tape collage assembled by Stapleton and McKenzie, ridden over by live electronics, voice, percussion, and a surreal theatrical instinct.

or as the band call it, “a collective groping”

aye.

items.body:
Described as a "musical poem", 'Mount Analogue' is a lengthy meditation on the works of avant-garde poet and writer René Daumal that's passed from Bill Laswell and P.St (plus an ensemble featuring Nils Petter Movaer, Anna Clementi, Hideo Yamaki and others) to guitarist Henry Kaiser.

'Mount Analogue' is named after Daumel's most well-known book, the self-styled "Novel of Symbolically Authentic Non-Euclidean Adventures in Mountain Climbing" that emerged almost a decade after his early death at just 36 in 1944. That text is excerpted here on the album-length title composition, that Czech experimental sort P.ST leads on electronics alongside Laswell, Kaiser, vocalists Clementi and Percy Howard, percussionist Yamaki, cornet player Graham Haynes, violinist Dorian Cheah, Keyboardist Peter Apfelbaum and Molvaer on trumpet. It was P.St who came up with the concept in the first place and his direction helps rein in such a wide spread of contributors; from the beginning, there's a sense of calm that's rarely ruptured. Washing pebbles are augmented by instrumental washes and a deep voice reading Daumal's words in English. "Seeing that I am nothing, I desire to become. Desiring to become, I live." reads Howard over Kaiser's tangled plucks. But it's Italian-Swedish singer Clementi's part that really takes this one to the next level, bounding acrobatically over the group's wash of instrumentation to paint in brighter colors before jazzy improvisations take root.

The second disc is handled exclusively by improv legend Kaiser, who spends almost an hour pondering Alejandro Jodorowsky's 'The Holy Mountain', a film that was directly inspired by Daumal's text, on the absorbing 'Jordorowsky's Peradam', before splitting off with a set of shorter solo jams. And on the digital version, P.St turns in an album length remix of the title track that's almost as good as the original, amping up the noise and the chaos without losing hold of the track's poetic cadence.

items.body:
Ostgut Ton’s freshest recruits trade in effortlessly rolling bleep techno and moodier meat motors primed to be played in the big house.

Along with the likes of Quelza and Inox Traxx, Berlin-based Justine Perry & Paula Kossi lend an injection of new blood to Berghain’s label revival. Their ‘Paired Works’ oscillate energies between Perry’s effervescent levity and Koski’s rolling momentum, with the latter at best on the stealth build of ‘Beyond the Line’ and finely poised, teasing pressure of ‘Opaline’, while Kossi best impresses with the concentrated, urgent canter of ‘Maeve’, with its plucky bassline, plus the dub chord-riding ‘Adnexa’, and Fadi Mohem-esque elegance of ‘Held in Place’.

items.body:
The jittery pulses and waking dream-like atmospheres of Dx2ov land on London’s Blank Mind for an album strafing between cut-up sound poetry and whisked garage-house.

“Dx2ov arrives on Blank Mind with Tonegues, his second vinyl LP following on from Interzona on Gost Zvuk in 2024. The LP title is a wordplay on the idea of speaking in tongues and sonic tonalities, echoing the process and dialogue that went into creating the record. Taken from a vast archive of material from 2019-2025, these ideas were arranged with the collaboration of label owner Sam Purcell and then completed with the long-distance assistance of Toupaz.

Tonegues is best seen through the lens of a beat-tape, with the playful flow and variety that the format provides, bursting with oddball ideas and punctuated with intangible vocal samples. Much like the LP’s beguiling, hand-drawn artwork by Wolfgang Matuschek, it is a glimpse into an inner world, a portal to somewhere uncanny and strange borne through imagination.

Light dub flourishes mix with footwork/IDM hybrids and understated, melancholic synthesis on ‘2018’, whilst the loose, rhythmic march of ‘Fon32’ evokes the dusty beatdown styles of early 2000s Detroit downtempo records. Whilst on one of the LP highlights ‘Trout’ he lays down a gleefully strange bed for the surrealist storytelling of Jacob Dwyer about interactions with dogs, dripping old houses and a perennial wish for the phone to ring with a heavy dub poetry slant. Dx2ov swiftly moves through more footwork adjacent, almost bedroom hyper-pop territories with a penchant for gabber kicks on ‘No Strings (feat DJ Paprika)’ and the maximalism of album closer 'Demetch' which continues in the tradition of wonky, mid-2010s UK bass music flips. The outcome is a confounding, unorthodox piece of work, zigzagging between forms, textures and moods.”

items.body:
Berlin’s lowkey ambient wunderkind follows on the promise of his acclaimed albums since 2018 - solo and as half of OCA - plus production for Kelela, with a lush study in Vibroacoustic therapy intended to help his parents sleep better.

The hour long suite stems from Florian TM Zeisig’s rare visit to his parents’ gaff in rural Bavaria a few years ago, where he discovered they had been using a vibroacoustic mattress - a mattress kitted with transducers or speakers - to aid them in getting some quality kip. Being a good lad, Florian wanted to help his parents in their quest, and spent the next few years developing this soundtrack; a serene 60’ of music resting on a rich bed of layered sub-bass frequencies that surely beckon users to the horizontal. 

Most sensitively tending to this premise, Zeisig takes his role with requisite amounts of conceptual seriousness and gently witted pathos that have come to define his work, as on the critically acclaimed OCA album ‘Aging’ with Yo van Lenz in 2018, and in 2020’s deeply charming ‘Coatcheck’ soundtrack for cloakroom assistants. Working within the “vibroacoustic” framework, his results are typically gorgeous and user-friendly, playing into the space between new age ambient music’s putative therapeutic purposes and its well intended pseudo-science, with a warmly sublime conception of classic ambient music that beautifully resonates with records from Eno to Space Afrika and Midori Takada.

items.body:
An advanced masterclass in Berlin beat science, ‘Wireless’ is the final and arguably strongest solo release by T++; aka Torsten Pröfrock, an artist with a long lineage of important releases under numrous aliases - Dynamo, Erosion,Log, Resilent, Traktor, Various Artists and more - a true pillar of Berlin's Techno legacy.

First issued by Honest Jon’s in 2010, the 2x12” features samples of singer and ndingidi-player Ssekinomu (originally found on the EMI archival dive ‘Bellyachers, Listen - Songs From East Africa, 1938-46’) reworked by Pröfrock into a volley of rambunctious but rudely disciplined club workouts some 75 years later. In many other hands, this could have been just another passable cut ’n splice edit, but T++ treats the material with a balance of reverence and raving license, highlighting an instinctive understanding of the original music's intent and purpose, and their deep rooted connection to modern fast rap and hardcore dance musics.

The four tracks amount to a contemporary classic in their field and also exist in a strong tradition of German artists ranging from Stockhausen to Can and Basic Channel whose music has crucially incorporated the fluid, rolling nature and spectra of African drumming patterns. However, it’s vital to point out that T++’s take on African drumming is also filtered thru a love of UK music - Jungle, D&B, garage, dubstep - meaning that his rhythms are properly underlined with syncopated, technoid basslines owing as much to Kingston, Jamaica as Brixton and Sheffield in the UK.

For anyone who had been intently listening to Pröfrock's output since his Traktor gems, thru his Dynamo aces, to early work with Monolake and his string of seminal T++ 12”s in the 2000’s, on its release in 2010 ‘Wireless’ quickly came to epitomise his approach to broken techno production at its most open-ended and inexorable. Between the itchy, sprung step of ‘Cropped’, the puckish darkside torque of ‘Anyi’, a voodoo communal in ‘Voice No Bodies’, and the reanimated spirits of ‘Dig’ you have some of the finest mutant techno ever cut to vinyl.

An absolute must-have for dancers and DJs.

items.body:
Whew! A who’s who of contemporary aces rework one of 2024’s strongest LPs, with everyone from Anderson Do Paraiso to Fauzia and Kelman Duran exerting canny spins on Nídia & Valentina’s sticks-meets-circuits polyrhythmic jams.

All hewing faithful to the originals, but delineated in compelling mix of club-ready styles, the remixers prove the classy contemporary mutability of ‘Estradas’ by dare-to-differ batida/tarraxho artist Nídia, and her prolific spar, Valentina Magaletti, who is resoundingly acclaimed for work with literally everyone in the modern scene. 

To play faves, DJ Anderson do Paraíso’s gothic baile spin on ‘Andiamo’ is a clear frontrunner, adding his own vox and illuminating bonds between Portuguese-speaking Afro-Latin diaspora, whilst Fauzia also kills with the glute-twang bassline of her ‘Nasty’ version, and Felt label boss Fergus Jones impresses with his dubbed-out slant on Valentina’s drumming in a ‘No Promises Version’.

Safe to say the rest do not let the side down, with Beyoncé producer Kelman Duran reframing ‘Ta A Bater Ya’ as a heady collage of after-the-storm ambient noise and spectral drums, and Rosa Pistola x Freebot proving ideal remixers for the horny sapphic twiss-up ‘Rapido’, and DJ Plead gets right entangled in the additional layers of percussion to his ’Sicilia Version’. Even Sherelle makes a noted progression from primary colour jungle to ruder, textured nuance on wicked 160BPM version of the title tune.

items.body:
French club music sculptor (Marine) Benabou comes into her own on a handful of rolling pressure systems backed with Kliche’s dub-diffused breakbeat remix.

Slotting very neatly into Blank Mind’s roster of sparing dance engineers - Lina Filipovich, Paperclip Minimiser, DJ ojo - the Berlin-based producer brings her background as mastering/cutting engineer at ManMade to the fore on a rangy EP. The precision-tooled, syncopated percussion and stereo-strafe grayscale movement of opener ‘Projet G’ establishes parameters where she moves freely into vaporised dub techno (‘Interlude’), to something approaching Sandwell District gone samba in ‘Rise’, and restless forms of sinuous, sidewinding suss in ’Shift’, while ‘Merge’ demonstrates her feel for lucid, resonant clarity and depth perception. Label mate Kliche flexes ‘Projet G’ in a dubbier antechamber style in step with DJ ojo aces.

items.body:
On a label full of weirdos, outliers, mavericks and freaks, clandestine Greek anomaly Aeson Zervas is Heat Crimes’ OG wildcard, landing a debut album a couple of years ago that sounded like The Caretaker channeling crates of rebetika, and now returning with this deeply elusive new LP of plasmic synths that unfolds in ways that will leave you with a proper motion sickness of time travel. Aye, it’s a special one.

After lighting up 2024 with blink ’n miss LP & tape drops, Aeson Zervas’s 3rd instalment dips into a perpetual night world of cobwebbed keyboard melodies and flame flicker incantations designed to score your next regression session. As ever, the label and artist remain tight-lipped about pretty much everything, but the vibe is self-evidently clammy and febrile thru a dozen parts familiar to both preceding drops, woven between pillars of inspiration in lemniscate loops and free flowing rhythmelodic arrangements that bind his ideas to bezonked minds.

The Mesolonghi-based enigma continues to prove a master of hypnosis and a conduit for ancient spirits seeping into the modern world, luring susceptible minds to states of bliss and dread, but not without that sense of romance that also lit up his prior releases. Once again feeling the same pull of past worlds as The Caretaker, only slanted to microtonal scales, his mix of lopped-off and extended melodies tell arcane stories still salient to contemporary imaginations able to tune in.

Activating with a section of meditative, almost no-wave strafing discord, themes of shimmering exotica slide into backyard ritualism, with a lilting marimba sounding like it escaped a Martin Denny side before bleeding into a Giallo-esque wheeze, thru port and island-hopping rebetika, and properly haunting passages of midnight sacred music swarmed by cicadas. The 6th (Χωρίς τίτλο 23) part of needling Italianate arps and screeches is particularly affective, as is the plugged-in folkdance sputter of the 8th (Χωρίς τίτλο 25), and a final couplet coming off like Muslimgauze with a thing for sleazy horror, not dub.

Basically, whatever this label serve, lap it up while you can.

items.body:
Tricky's most confident full-length since the 1990s, 'Different When It's Silent' is a dark, painful and melancholy reflection on decades spent in the spotlight and the tragic death of his daughter.

Tricky was never particularly chuffed with the term "trip-hop". Even back in the '90s he bristled at its mention, telling Melody Maker he'd "fucking deny having anything to do with it." And since then he's preferred to stake his claim as a perpetual outsider, jokingly calling his music "Tricky-hop" instead. But you can't deny his influence on the genre: here's an artist who was working with legendary Bristolian sound system the Wild Bunch before he was out of school and joined Massive Attack when he was still a teen, all this before going on to pen one of the genre's core texts. Even as the '90s drew to a close, trip-hop's oily early essence had been swapped out for the relative candyfloss of Morcheeba, Sneaker Pimps and Zero 7. And now, the genre's a catchall term - used to describe Eartheater, Erika de Casier, James K... even FKA twigs. You probably see why Tricky was so reticent to take the label seriously.

Because in 2026, trip-hop's meaning has shifted but Tricky really hasn't. He's still working with roughly the same elements, projecting his will into tracks that sound as if they're trapped between rocks and hard places from across the musical quarry: metal, rap, dub, industrial music. You'll notice a conspicuous absence of lounge or acid jazz. "Make me wanna die," groans vocalist Mitch Sanders on the opening track, echoing Martina Toppley Bird's delivery on the 'Pre-Millennium Tension' masterpiece. Sanders is a new voice for Tricky, but comes from familiar soil, the Bristol-born son of one of his closest friends. And he's a good conduit for Tricky's emotions. Starting with a callback to his most crucial material, Tricky is making a connection that holds up, too - 'Different When It's Silent' sounds like the Tricky album many of us were expecting to appear in the wake of 'Angels With Dirty Faces'.

It's an album of songs, not just ideas, and Tricky's hoarse voice is there like an omnipresent force in the background, growling next to Sanders' own. On 'Be Still in the Pain' he falls into a ghostly falsetto that fills the top end next to Tricky's wormy analog synth bass and skippy beat, but it's Run Red Rambo, another Bristol talent who helps tie this one together, laying down a rap that perfectly contrasts the other two vocals. And Tricky's hooks still hit hard when they need to - the tear-inducing chorus on 'Paris Maybe' or the druggy callback to a world before Britpop on 'I'm Yours'. And it all comes to a head on the finale, when Tricky brings back Polish singer Marta Złakowska for a track that directly addresses the death of his daughter in 2019. "It's a great way to end the album," he explains in the accompanying press release. "And then I can move on to other things."

items.body:
Shadowy São Paulo-based producer Iguana, who helped define last year's sub-underground with the brilliant 'Escama', returns to the Acta label with another advanced transmission, chipping away at the funk ritmado sound with dizzying electroacoustic percussion and vortex'd samples. RIYL xavisphone, DJ Ramon Successo, Arca or RHR.

Harboring some of the world's most innovative club music, Brazil is developing hybridised sub-genres at a rapid pace, so it stands to reason that the country's underground should be just as vital. Look just beneath the surface and you'll come across Acta, the label that brought us records from local alchemists Yvu, DIGESTIVO and Iguana and reached out to the wider world on last year's excellent 'Caudal' compilation, connecting with like minds Ship Sket, ZULI, Gyrofield and others. And 'CHORA' continues the narrative, building on São Paulo's galvanic funk ritmado sound, a more syncopated, percussion-heavy variant that contrasts the carnivalesque bruxaria style of the city's southernmost parties.

Over in just two-and-a-half minutes, Iguana's title track plays like a flex, showcasing the producer's sound design skills in a whirlwind of metallic, rusted hits and corroded vocal cuts. It owes as much to SOPHIE's 'Faceshopping' or Arca's earliest, gooiest gear as it does to São Paulo, neatly juxtaposing its ear-splitting distortions with subversive, rubber-clad rhythmic experimentation. If you're into purer ritmado sounds, Iguana's got you covered with two even more percussive variations, a rattly version that adds cloudy West Asian string samples and an all drums edit that might be the best of the bunch, tickling the original rhythm with hologramatic hand drum syncopations and 'Cichlisuite'-level sonic whirlpools.

If that's not enough, Yvu weighs in with a ruggedly psychoactive remix, slowing the original down and tweezing out the beats, icing up the dead space with dubwise echoes and alien interferences. Serious dirt fer the heads.

items.body:
Using no synths whatsoever, iconic Mute sound engineer Paul Kendall (Depeche Mode, Recoil, Nitzer Ebb) refines his industrial concrète concept on a second Downwards LP, sampling domestic objects (radiators, flasks, shelves) and emerging with grinding, distorted rhythmic gear that ends up somewhere between Pan Sonic, Phoenecia, General Magic & Pita’s ‘Fridge Trax’.

Kendall cut his teeth in Daniel Miller's Worldwide International studio, engineering for Nitzer Ebb, Wire, Depeche Mode, Recoil and countless others, eventually setting up a short-lived but excellent Mute sub-label The Parallel Series. Following years of close work with Alan Wilder on Recoil material, his 2021 debut for Downwards 'Boundary Macro' made use of an of array of microphones to zoom into various objects' hidden facets, essentially mimicking macro photography by using unusual amplifications to produce rusted rhythms and heavily weathered textures. On ‘AMENACE, goodbye’, he repeats the process but with an array of domestic appliances and objects, leaving pretty much no recognisable trace of the source material by the time he’s finished the process.

Kendall stretches and squeezes his recordings, playing fast and loose with powdery bit-crushed beats and time-stretched blips that are almost too destroyed to make head nor tail of. On opener 'Orgone’, he extracts and loops the recordings to create its own loping rhythm in a mode you might confuse for one of Justin Broadrick's soundsystem-ripping experiments or an unreleased DJ Scud proof-of-concept. Tune in, though, and the full spectrum pops into view: the music's concrète components don't just add texture, they're the glue, the air, the movement itself. By magnifying unheard intimate sounds, Kendall makes the humdrum as menacing as the world beneath the white picket fence in the intro of David Lynch's 'Blue Velvet'. Lock into 'Reset', a whirr of subterranean rumbles and half-hallucinated drones that's as brain-melting as anything on Phoenecia's ketamine-fueled 'Brownout'. Or the fully disorienting 'Diminish', a reduced Pan Sonic-style belter that sounds as if it's being played through the reinforced walls of a bomb shelter.

How can the perception of time—both for the listener and the performers—be turne
items.body:
Egil Kalman chases a string of inventive iDEAL LPs with fresh, variegated slants on the space between free jazz, folk, and electronics, weaving modular synths with lithe double bass and Jew’s harp, also performed by drummer Hans Hulbaekmo, across gently tumultuous soundscapes and radiant groovers.

“With Unit of Time, Hans Hulbækmo and Egil Kalman aim to show that we can experience the essence of time through rhythm. How can the perception of time—both for the listener and the performers—be turned completely on its head by rhythm? By zooming in on rhythms from traditional music from around the world, the hyper-focused interplay of free jazz, and the rhythmic structures of just-intoned drone music (which is essentially about resonant intervals built on polyrhythms), these gentlemen create a wholly unique rhythmic universe—a universe where both listeners and performers can lose themselves in a thicket of twisted branches.

As you know, Motvind Records is much about filling out our own record collections, and it’s high time for a drum’n’bass record that you can enjoy on the couch at home. Piercing the Veil by William Parker and Hamid Drake is fantastic, but it’s 25 years old... Now, we finally have another album where the groove button is stuck in the "on" position, and creativity overflows.

"The rhythm section" has long had a supporting role in rhythmic music like jazz, pop, and rock, often overshadowed by a brash saxophonist, lead guitarist, or singer dominating most of the frequency range. In jazz, much happened early on with drummers like Max Roach, Kenny Clarke, and Warren "Baby" Dodds, as well as bassists like Jimmy Blanton, Charles Mingus, and Scott LaFaro. In folk music traditions with strong rhythmic elements, such as those in Africa and Southeast Asia, these instruments have played a more prominent role in shaping the music. But all too often, especially in Norwegian folk music, these instruments have had a rather static function. In my own record collection, I even have an album where the accompanying musicians aren’t credited—it just says, "Ola Opheim, fiddle w/Rhythm."

However, Hans Hulbækmo and Egil Kalman have long been a playful and creative rhythm section, with one foot in free jazz and the other in folk music. They’ve played together in the Marthe Lea Band and other projects, and since last year, they’ve delved into the folk music of Norway and Sweden—all set in an experimental duo format: drums and mouth harp (Hans) meet modular synth and double bass and mouth harp (Egil). They’ve now gone deeper into this, aiming to create an album they can take on tour. Both individually and together, they have explored folk music, jazz, and experimental electronic music. Their projects, such as Hulbækmo & Jacobsen Familieorkester, Skrekk & Guro, Camilla Hole Trio, and Reolô, showcase their diverse musical backgrounds. In this duo project, they draw from rhythmic details in folk music—small elements that form the basis for minimalist compositions full of improvisation.

They have composed and improvised most of the material, including a traditional tune from Setesdal, Filleværen. The album is a good old-fashioned musical journey where all the tracks have distinct characteristics yet are strangely interconnected. The music is also highly visual. Once the record has spun through once, it’s tempting to flip it over again—once you get a taste for good music, it’s hard to stop. And they don’t let the groove dictate everything. Some melodies are interpreted more straightforwardly, but the unconventional instruments they use give the music a different kind of depth. Unusual timbres and sonic phenomena emerge, giving the music a hypnotic quality. Both the listener and the musicians themselves can get lost in the groove, immersed in a rhythmic cosmos.”

items.body:
Previously released on Low Company in 2023, Purely Physical Teeny Tapes reissue the full album from Tarquin Manek, one of the most prolific, distinct and perhaps under-recognised producers in our orbit. If bezonked, subaquatic dub-pop zoners are your thing, anything from The Skaters to Swell Maps, YL Hooi to Carla dal Forno, CS + Kreme to Jac Berrocal, this one’s for you.

The 16th and final number from short-lived yet beloved London shop-turned-label Low Company renders a raft of works made by Tarquin Manek (F Ingers, Kallista Kult, Tarcar) 2013-2020, and shafted in the release schedule until now. Nine songs depict Tarquin in his soggiest songwriting mode, floating over rugged, groggy loops in a rare, non-collaborative form. It’s a captivating self-portrait of an artist who is perhaps best known for his collaborations and work behind the scenes, variously fostering talents from the Naarm (Melbourne) undergrowth such as YL Hooi and Carla dal Forno, the latter of whom was his bandmate in F Ingers alongside Sam Karmel of CS + Kreme, and many of whom would grace Low Company and its cult predecessor Blackest Ever Black. 

A sense of desiccated bliss riddles the bittersweet fantasy tang of ‘Breathing Under Honey’, where Manek sets a course from the bleached coral underfoot on ‘Stones on the Beach’, to a lizard-hipped bossa shuffle on ‘Mirage Game’, via superb bouts of Count Ossie-meets-Spencer Clark whims on ’Submerging Emergency’, thru Hassellian trumpet gargling in the sink on ‘Sea Slug Bender’, to instrumental cyberpunk sea shanty, ‘Age Old Squall’, or coming across Lewis on a jolly with drunken sailors at a late night Berlin bar on ‘Basic Trouble’.

Of course it all hits that crinkled sweetspot for levels of eyes-half-shut perpendicular pop that we’ve come to expect from Low Company and their constellation of affiliates, joining dots between the ahead-of-their-time ‘80s post punk tape oddities that surface on Efficient Space, A Colourful Storm’s febrile dream sequences, to rickety DIY bops from the London mulch.

Laters, Low Company - a proper bunch of sound cnuts.

What followed was less a traditional writing process than a shared unfolding – an instinctive, immersive exchange that stretched across geographies, time zones, and states of being. The duo first met in June 2024 in North Carolina, brought together by a
items.body:
Helado Tropical, the debut collaborative album from Helado Negro and Reyna Tropical.

"It didn’t begin with a plan so much as a meeting: two artists orbiting similar questions around language, identity, and music, finally landing in the same room. What followed was less a traditional writing process than a shared unfolding – an instinctive, immersive exchange that stretched across geographies, time zones, and states of being.

The duo first met in June 2024 in North Carolina, brought together by a mutual friend and a loose invitation to spend time in the studio. What might have been a brief session turned into something closer to a three-day sleepover – equal parts conversation, curiosity, and creative risk. Reyna Tropical, accustomed to close-knit collaborations, stepped into new creative territory, while Helado Negro brought a similar sense of curiosity and fluidity.

What emerged was immediate, rather than easing into collaboration, the two found themselves propelled forward by it – building songs in real time, responding to each other’s instincts without over-explaining them. There was no rigid division of roles. One would begin an idea, the other would answer. A melody would suggest a rhythm; a rhythm would reshape a lyric.

Across Helado Tropical, there is a noticeable absence of constraint: not just musically, but conceptually. Both artists share a long-standing resistance to the expectations often placed on Latin music: what it should sound like, how it should feel, what stories it should tell. As they do individually, these two artists create space for something more fluid and personal on this project.

What makes Helado Tropical particularly resonant is the sense of trust that underpins it. Trust in each other, of course, but also trust in instinct and in the process. Much of the album was written through improvisation, with meaning revealing itself only later, as the artists listened back and reflected."

items.body:
Steve Gurley and co.’s deeply inspirational run of ’92-’93 hardcore jungle 12”s as Foul Play, compiled on a deadly doublepack via Bristol-via-Berlin torch carriers, Sneaker Social Club.

‘Origins’ contains some of the greatest music of the early ‘90s, particularly spotlighting the transition from rave’s rugged building blocks into artfully hi-tech dance music during that pivotal period. Sifting gems from both volumes of Foul Play’s early EPs on Oblivion Records - including the all-timers ‘Dubbing You’ and ‘Ricochet’ - plus an early 12” for Moving Shadow, the set documents breakbeat hardcore hitting a creative zenith of hyper-chopped soul, dub and pop samples arranged with staccato stabs, cut-up, shuffling breaks and drum machines, right in the pocket before it was codified as jungle. 

Thanks to the studio ingenuity of Steve Gurley, who cut his teeth on these recordings, the set can also be heard to characterise the development of what is known as the hardcore continuum, as defined in Gurley’s subsequent shift into jungle, proper, and then UKG - the ultimate refinement of hardcore’s 2-step shuffles and sexy swerve. The seeds of enduring styles & patterns to come are sown here, from the fractious rush of ‘Finest Illusion’ through the haunting zinger ‘Dubbing You’, to the needlepoint discipline of ‘Ricochet’ and effortless, toes-off-the-floor skip and parry of ‘Screwface’, to the jump-up jungle blueprint ‘Ragatere’.

Alltimers, the lot of them.

items.body:
Psychedelic sorcerers Nuke Watch return with a definitive blast of improvised studio shenanigans on London’s Sagome, after celebrated turns with TTT, PPM, and patience. Proper outerzone madness, tipped FFO Pekka Airaksinen, Wolf Eyes, Marshall Allen, Sperm.

Expanding from a duo to a trio with the addition of Zack Stafford on wind and electronics, Nuke Watch emulate the effects of some legit Lucy for a particularly skewiff and trippy session on their 8th studio album ‘Fusion’. The key to the LP is in the titular nod to psych jazz and rock hybrids of the ‘70s, where styles began to melt into one another via the extraordinary musical virtuosity of the likes of King Crimson, Tony Williams, and John McLaughlin. But rather than overly intricate key changes and showmanship, Nuke Watch distill a confluence of inspirations - contemporary urban beats, dub, trip metal, outernational trance, US basement noise, raga drone - with an alchemic, imaginative ingenuity they can safely call their own. 

The trio, plus the likes of Daryl Seaver on EWI MIDI and instrument, a la Marshall Allen or Wolf Eyes, giive it hot and sticky with a flow of intuitive ideas best representing a prolific creative practice of open-ended jams. But again, they deftly sidestep the more hoary connotations of psych with a freezer fresh zing and grasp of groove that, just about, lets us know it’s the 2020s, not the 1970s, or at least somewhere along that timeline. This uchronic approach, factored by extramusical prompts from psyops, eschatology, and contemporary political clusterfucks, yields a brace of hypnotic, hallucinatory projections in progression from the swingeing groove and smeared apparitions of the opener, thru the mutant raga of the ‘War Lock’ section, to a properly unbuckled ‘New American Psycho’ movement squirming in space between Sperm and Wolf Eyes’ trip metal.

items.body:
Debut EP of raw drone techno minimalism by London-based Brazilian artist Protocol, doubling as the first entry on his label, interiør, and advised FFO Pan Sonic, CUB, SM-LL, Zhark’s Huren & Kareem.

Recorded ’25-’26, ‘Channel Zero’ feels like staring at snow on an analog tele while the warehouse next door hosts an Eraserhead-themed industrial rave. Ascetic to the bone, it unfurls four starkly reverberant variants of unsteady bass thrum and gloaming atmospheres; emerging from a grayscale blizzard into quaking echoes of early Zhark Records on ‘Lost Signal (Noise)’, and wielding the kicks offbeat against unyielding, gnawing spectral tones in ‘Blind Belief’. We’re most partial to the sleepwalker techno momentum of ‘Electromagnetic Shadow’, pairing gaunt, hovering drone with a pendulous bass march, while ‘Black Snow Cult’ palpitates like Regis & Mønic’s cult CUB duo.

items.body:
Sylvain Chauveau's first album since 2022's 'L'effet rebond', 'The Complexity of the Simple' is inspired by a Zen garden, a set of lovingly handcrafted minimal instrumentals that took 10 years to properly shape.

Chauveau was marveling at the lines drawn in the gravel of Kyoto's Tokaian temple when the idea for 'The Complexity of the Simple' appeared. He's been refining (and reducing) his sound for decades now - his last set was called 'Ultra-minimal' - but there's a different level of focus on display here, something controlled and, if not emotionless, then at least contemplative. By stripping away the fat of romance and aesthetic grandstanding from his earlier material, Chauveau has found a niche that's as peaceful and philosophically absorbing as that Zen garden. And, considering a future without fossil fuels and the producing, playing and listening that new era might provoke, he engages in a push and pull with sound that's engaging without being mawkish.

'Le Zen Dans L'Art Du Tir À L'Arc' transports us to Kyoto with its measured rhythmelodic chimes - from handpan, glockenspiel and synth - and on 'The Guitar Piece I Wrote for Masumi', Chauveau plays his instrument so softly that it almost evaporates. On 'Wabi Sabi for Beginners', he layers warbling synth tones on top of each other, creating beating rhythms that only appear if you're really tuning in, and on the final track 'Lignes Tranquilles Dans Le Gravier Blanc', he's joined by Tetuzi Akiyama on acoustic guitar and his longtime spar Cyril Secq, who follow his lead, playing lowercase notes into tempered radio interference and subtle, almost imperceptible environmental recordings.

items.body:
OG post-dubstep mutator Untold flexes his range in lithe, stepping techno and offbeat bruk modes for his Hemlock Recordings.

After finding his feet in the club again with ‘HEK036’, the English artist serves all points of the night with suggestive options for dance on the ‘False Vacuum EP’. It’s a return to the sort of restlessly inventive energy that he seemed to run out of at the end of the ‘00s, a decade he was instrumental in shaping from the post-UKF and grime years forward, with a recombinant approach to fusing UKG with everything from Mexican tribal guarachara to electronica, before promptly departing stage left until a 2023 EP with Parris.

Back on it with a custom-refined palette and focussed zeal, he spins the club from a sort of Latinate minimal techno-step strapped with booming subs and delicate keys on ‘Last Day of The Bluebells’, thru a killer bit of dark UKG/breakstep rufige tooled with discordant electronics on ‘Eyeballed’, into Joe-style polyrhythms on ‘Three Finger Test’. His feel for unusual syncopation prompt brukstep oddness in ‘Lyall’s Wren’, and ultimately the EP’s finest showcase of shearing sound designer tekkerz and chamber classical keys goes like some early Arovane on ‘Worse Than I Thought’.

items.body:
A second pressing of last year’s gorgeous fourth and final album from Old Saw, the American Primitive project of Tongue Depressor's Henry Birdsey, riffing on the classic Takoma paradigm with additional ferric washes and layered instrumental drones, huge recommendation if yr into Bruce Langhorne’s ‘The Hired Hand’ or classic work by Daniel Lanois, Laraaji, Pelt, Stars Of The Lid, State River Widening.

'The Wringing Cloth' is Birdsey’s fourth and final Old Saw outing, and ironically it’s also the one that has garnered most amount of critical and commercial success. Old Saw’s shimmering, drone-heavy soundscapes were recorded on 1/4" tape at various locations in New England over the last few years and are once again paired with evocative black and white imagery from photographer Dylan Hausthor, whose landscapes somehow perfectly capture the timeless, widescreen appeal of the music inside.

Birdsey's pedal, lap steel and resonator are at the core of each track, but the album also features Old Saw’s usual personnel; Harper Reed on nylon string guitar and banjo, Ira Dorset on fiddle and bowed strings, Ann Rowlis on reed organ and harmonium, Jim Cutler on telecaster, Addison Starkweather-Price on bass, and Peter Catchpole on metal objects and power hammer. That lap steel lends the music its stylistic anchor, taking us through decades of American folk before gently fraying at the edges. Birdsey's application of classical minimalism - the themes that surge through his work with Zach Rowden as Tongue Depressor - is still somehow present here, especially as the record pulls into its second side and the shimmering country-fied atmosphere is pierced with bell-like sounds, but the overall mood and flavour of the record is distinctly easy on the ear and timeless in its appeal.

As the label put it, “What has always been uncanny about this music is that it arrives in a state at once familiar and obscured, like a memory weighed down with sensory information but no identifying details to place it. The Wringing Cloth walks off further into that geographical dream without time or language, until it’s just a speck of light….”

items.body:
Berlin-based sound artist and composer Jana Irmert, who was last spotted pairing up with 7038634357 on the Portals GRM split series, explores the deep underground on her soundtrack to Jeffrey Zablotny's 'Messengers', blending sounds from a vintage Yamaha Electone organ with seismic recordings and materials resonances.

Irmert's work often examines unseen, or at least unheard realms; her last side, 'Portals', presented the sounds we least expect to hear from a rainforest, using ultrasound microphones to capture imperceptible high frequency sonics. So she seems like the ideal choice to score 'Messengers', a documentary that looks at three hidden underground research centers that study "the universe's most elusive phenomena". And Irmert's treatment is undoubtedly smart, using the wheezing Electone sounds - including the clucks of the keys and the air in the pumps - to represent the fragility of humanity against the backdrop of overpoweringly dense sounds she sources from "natural materials" and recordings of seismic activity.

It's hard to get an accurate view of what we're hearing without the film or detailed notes, but regardless, Irmert writes a soundtrack that's surprisingly absorbing, resisting the temptation to weigh it down with the usual dark ambient cues. Instead, her atmospheric elements are held in place by the Electone's warbling drones, elements that just gently hint at sci-fi without going full 'Stranger Things'. It's smart stuff that makes us curious about not just the film but the subterranean observatories themselves.

items.body:
Sickest Dagbani dance-pop from northern Ghana, all produced by Mohamed “Ebony” Fuseini of Studio Simpa, and voiced by Dickson Gawani, Bala Zaaku, and Yaa Naara, among others - FFO DJ Tobzy, DJ Diaki, Nozinja, Music From Saharan WhatsApp

Issued on the Autotune The World label that shares its name with Chris Kirkley's long-running NTS show, ‘Digital Dance Music on VCD from Dagbon, Northern Ghana’ follows the show and label’s hyper-specific focus on the likes of Tecnobrega from Brasil and Caribbean Soca & Chutney with a rare jag upcountry in Ghana’s predominantly Muslim north. 

Armed with phone mic, FL Studio, and the best local singers on speed dial, Mohamed “Ebony” Fuseini updates local styles of Dagbani dance rhythm and melody with shiny VSTs and, of course, nuff autotune, to bring the rural sound closer to those from bigger cities, as heard on shared mp3s and physical media such as VCDs.

Available and traded at local markets, but rarely heard by international ears, those VCDs feature footage of women shaking hips - a “light cultural transgression” in the mostly Muslim area - with lyrics by local “Gawani”, flashy singers such as Dickson Gawani, Bala Zaaku, and Yaa Naara, with something to show, and matched by the energy of Ebony’s productions. Not as rushy as, say DJ Tobzy from Lagos, or DJ Diaki in Mali, Ebony’s Studio Simpa cuts are more melodic, pop-wise, maybe best compared with the colourful hi-energy of Shangaan Electro, heard on highlights from Dickson Gawani’s acidic percolator ‘So Tinha’ (also in a killer 12” bonus mix!), thru the lilting ballad ‘Baamunu’ by Obaako, to the unique skank of Aminu Dakogu, and the supremely light-headed effect of ‘M Be Adama’ by Alhassan Kukuonaa - all primed to light a fire on summer ’26 ‘floors.

items.body:
In their sublime duo debut the simpatico synth & guitar of Jonny Nash & Tomo Katsurada is seduces to blissed, wind-whispering soundscapes, hashed out over the course of 12 months since Katsurada lent strings to Nash’s ‘Once Was Our Forever’. Dream material FFO Yuta Matsumura, Tenniscoats, Durutti Column...

"Netherlands-based artists Tomo Katsurada (Ex-Kikagaku Moyo / Future Days Radio) and Jonny Nash (Melody As Truth) combine forces for an exploration into the sonic potential of the guitar duo, rooted in their experiences performing together over the last 12 months.

Friends and admirers of each other’s work for a decade, their musical collaboration began in 2024 with Katsurada asking Nash to contribute guitar to his debut EP ‘Dream Of The Egg’. Sensing the need to explore this further, they spent the following year performing together in different configurations, with Nash joining Katsurada’s trio and Katsurada in turn playing with Nash as a duo, across a wide spectrum of spaces, from churches and temples to concert halls, theatres and outdoor festivals. With new ideas developing organically out of these performances, recording new material became the next logical step. A short period of three days was set aside with a clear goal: to capture the essence of their fluid, intertwining melodies and guitar playing in a way that felt as direct and unfiltered as possible. Working from a handful of pre-existing sketches, they left ample room for experimentation to unfold within the process.

The results are presented on ‘At The Emerald Pool’, a collection of ten pieces that offer the listener a full immersion into the pair’s sound. With guitar as the primary instrument for both artists, it is no surprise that the core of the album lies here, specifically in the fluid interplay between the two players. Layers of gentle, delay-soaked fingerpicking often make it almost impossible to distinguish where one player ends and the other begins. As soloists, both Katsurada and Nash have a gift for crafting melodic lines that feel open and ascending, expressive and hopeful without becoming saccharine. Longer, more abstract pieces are counterbalanced by a series of shorter songs, with five vocal tracks appearing across the album. The decision to share vocal duties lends the record a unique quality and a strong sense of variation, bringing a wide expressive range out of a deliberately focused musical framework.

‘At The Emerald Pool’ represents the first chapter in an ongoing musical dialogue, an attempt to capture a moment of connection, openness and discovery, laying the foundation for what continues to unfold."

items.excerpt: Music From Memory chase their cherished survey of 90s ambient techno with a sparkling set of its Japanese echoes little known beyond its domestic market compiled by Jamie Tiller (RIP) and Eiji Taniguchi - consider it a guided tour to a parallel dimension, primed for the gouch out and lucid dreaming. items.body:
Music From Memory chase their cherished survey of 90s ambient techno with a sparkling set of its Japanese echoes little known beyond its domestic market compiled by Jamie Tiller (RIP) and Eiji Taniguchi - consider it a guided tour to a parallel dimension, primed for the gouch out and lucid dreaming.

Flush with fluttering arps and sanguine grooves, ’Virtual Dreams II - Ambient Explorations 1993-1999’ scans a familiar yet oddly distant sound adjacent to the formative sounds of Warp’s AI series and a whole cohort of ‘90s Western producers. Harvested from Music From Memory’s vast shelves, they introduce the lay ambient fan to a raft of names hardly known beyond their homeland, who still float the imagination to the horizontal and sublime with their contribution to a double refractive dialogue of electronic music influence mutated in translation between East and West since the ‘70s.

Smooth around the edges and clear-eyed in their quest for lushness, all 13 artists share a blissed pathos and effortlessness of execution that will see this set travel to collections across the world. In sequence from the nine minutes of near beat-less burble to ‘Blown Fruit’ by Dub Squad, and thru the twelve minute evocation of Eno or Vangelis’ Bladerunner score in Buddhastick Transparent’s ‘Eras (666)’, they limn a emotive and gently arc taking in Red Planet synth whistles and tactful acid squirm of Akio / Okihide’s ‘Phoenix At Desert’, the chiming carillon of Ambient 7’s ‘Escape’ recalling early Bedouin Ascent and Orbital, 

Yukihiro Fukutomi’s centrepiece ‘5 Blind Boys’ can be heard to bridge the prevailing influence of Japanese environmental ambient with its new green shoots in the ’90s, whilst the likes of Web with a slinky ‘The Cycle of Seasons’ remind to analogs in early Dave Mousing and The Black Dog, along with the air-stepping bliss out ‘Pause’ by Katsuya Hironaka. Fans of Susumu Yokota’s early ‘90s gliders will be in their element with Riow Arai’s shine-eyed ’1969’, and likewise fall for the string laden sashay of ‘Sbow Bird’ by Modern Living, and the oh so demure Carl Craig-via-Paddy McAloon sentiment of ‘Poisson D’Avril (Galaxy Dub)’ by Missing Project. Trust it would take years and wads of dosh to source all this stuff yourself, let MFM do the hard work for ya.

items.body:
FELT survey Copenhagen's contemporary jazz scene with RMC graduate Vincent Yuen Ruiz’s intimate and strikingly minimal rendition of stifled percussion, spacious piano and precise double bass work, tipped FFO of The Necks x Talk Talk, naturally.

Ruiz is a seasoned jazz player who's also nursed a parallel reputation as a post-rocker, formerly playing bass in Plaistow. And it's this knowledge of a world outside of jazz that gives 'Trio' its edge. It's not a post-rock record, by any means, but it's not pure jazz either - or at least, it doesn't sound as if it's confined by the aesthetic. The ensemble formed in 2019, but their last record together, 2021's 'Le seul salut que je connaisse', was recorded as a six-piece. Ruiz strips the sound to its bare bones on 'Trio', relying on unusual percussive sounds (provided by drummer Anders Vestergaard) to fill in some of the gaps. And although Rasmus Kjær takes a de facto lead roll on piano, it's the rhythm section, commanded by Ruiz on double bass, that makes 'Trio' so fascinating.

There's an almost meditative sense of calm to opener 'Choral', with Vestergaard's bowed cymbal tones providing a neat bed for Kjær's Bach and Ravel-inspired flourishes. The tension is only released when Ruiz's soft bass enters the frame, played somewhere between improvisation and composition, minimalism and decelerated chamber jazz. Just as he slimmed down his ensemble, Ruiz slims down the pieces themselves, condensing and distilling his ideas so the record never gets busy, or outstays its welcome. Just head to the  central piece 'Weaving', beautifully balancing its measured piano with Vestergaard's odd flurries of percussion that sometimes appear for just a second.

We can hear post-rock - particularly the variety that Talk Talk perfected - but our brains are also directed into filling in the gaps. 'Trio' is an album that lives and dies on its pauses, focusing on decaying notes and echoing rhythms in all their quiet beauty.

items.body:
An extra sugary batch of queer cult pop fancies on Cairo’s ever-wonderful Nashazphone label; super melodic, passionate synth-pop songs about boys, beauty and the melancholy of youth, tipped for fans of Elli et Jacno, Taxi Girl and Mathematiques Modernes.

‘Hélas’ collects 15 songs from the repertoire of Neoboris, an infamous Bordeaux/Pau duo highly active in the late ‘90s and early ‘00s. Drawing on direct Punk, Wave, Rave Culture and “Variété Française” influences, it functions as a perfect time capsule of a very specific era and mood: a boy-and-girl duo celebrating their love for boys, with melancholy and beauty.

"The origin story reads like an archetype, but the details make it sting. One half of Neoboris came out of hardcore raves and Bordeaux punk bands, carrying the raw‑throated urgency of that milieu; the other, Boris, grew up on New Wave and goth, a born songwriter whose melancholic streak ran as deep as his knack for hooks. Together they found a common altar in Elli et Jacno, Taxi Girl, Mathématiques Modernes – that peculiarly French intersection where cheap drum machines, fragile synth lines and deadpan vocals can suddenly break your heart. Out of that devotion came a duo aesthetic: compact songs, simple structures, lyrics that flirt with kitsch and then side‑step into something sharper, all delivered with the kind of chemistry you can’t rehearse into existence.

Their shows were wild in the way that only under‑funded, over‑feeling gigs can be: feedback squeal, rushed tempos, voices occasionally cracking, the two of them radiating that mix of shyness and bravado you get when you’re singing your secrets out loud. Hélas gathers the studio and home‑recorded echoes of that era and orders them into an emotional arc – from rush to comedown, infatuation to regret, celebration to elegy. The production sits right on the fault line between DIY and pop: drum machines slightly out of time, synth presets pushed into unexpected shapes, guitars toggling between brittle and blissed, all wrapped around melodies that would sound just as right on a transistor radio as in a squat.

The shadow that hangs over the record is Boris’s death in 2008, a break so abrupt it turned the entire project into unfinished business. The surviving member’s decision to keep singing these songs “everywhere I can” isn’t nostalgia, it’s a refusal to let that voice vanish into footnote status. Hélas makes that refusal tangible: 15 tracks that re‑situate Neoboris not as local cult trivia but as part of a larger, messy history of queer‑coded, under‑the‑radar French pop. You hear the mourning in the title, of course, but the music itself leans hard into joy – messy, melancholy, shoulder‑to‑shoulder joy, the kind you find on cramped dance floors at four in the morning. Singing with him then, now, and forever: Hélas documents that promise in all its scruffy, luminous detail."

items.body: Label: Self released, 2026 Personnel - Jay Matharu: guitar, keys; Erik Brandell: tenor saxophone; Christine Lanusse: bass guitar; Jacob Johnson: drums. Jay Matharu is an eclectic British-born guitarist and composer living in Uppsala, Sweden. His bold sound reflects a strong connection to metal—he’s a member of the band Liv Sin—but Disillusion marks a turning point in his solo career, weaving prog-rock, fusion, jazz-funk, and R&B into a patchwork of influences shaped through carefully crafted arrangements. Each member of his quartet—tenor saxophonist Erik Brandell, bassist Christine Lanusse, and drummer Jacob Johnson—recorded the album’s eight original compositions remotely. The music emerged from Matharu’s Master’s research in Music Performance. “ Atrophy ” is introduced in waltz time by Matharu, who is soon joined by Brandell as the music pivots into a 4/4 funk excursion. Both musicians splash a multitude of colors across the fluid rhythmic tapestry before returning to the opening 3/4 meter. “ Bare ” keeps the ternary feel alive, aligning saxophone and guitar in stimulating parallel lines. Brandell’s solo, imbued with adventurous melody, eloquence, and energy, invites us into compelling jazz fusion territory. “ Cog ” reveals classical influences within a theme receptive to subtle tempo shifts. Johnson’s snappy drum fills carry a prog-rock attitude, pairing naturally with Lanusse’s popping bass grooves. The piece is fueled by Matharu’s chromatic runs in a thought-provoking meeting point between Joe Satriani and Rez Abbasi. The Indo-jazz-rock thread runs even deeper in “ Chalo ”, a kaleidoscopic mosaic unfolding through ten-beat cycles and paying tribute to Matharu’s late mentor, sitar player Pandit Sanjay Guha. While “ Deluge ” features a memorable theme, a touch of Latin elation, and the bandleader’s metal-inflected soloing, “ Butterflies ” is a rewarding odd-metered exercise driven by throbbing bass lines and strong melodic development. The blazing guitar solo unfolds over a septuple-meter backdrop before launching into a metal-jazz romp fueled with high-octane energy. Throughout the album, Matharu and his band periodically reinvigorate the proceedings, with the closing “ Bittersweet ” standing as another fine example of dramatic shifts in rhythm and mood, moving from R&B soulfulness to jazz-funk audacity while leaving ample room for the drummer to stretch out. Although the ideas on Disillusion emerged from improvisational exploration, the whole outshines the parts. Matharu is following a promising path. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Atrophy ► 02 - Bare ► 07 - Butterflies
